entities.name: AFRO Archives (Afro Charities)
entities.description: The archive of the Baltimore AFRO-American Newspapers, managed by the nonprofit Afro Charities; one of the largest intact Black-newspaper photo and paper collections still held by its publisher's community.

claims.claim: Afro Charities manages the AFRO Archives, the repository of the AFRO American Newspapers (founded 1892 in Baltimore), holding thousands of original AFRO newspapers, more than 3 million photographs, rare audio/visual materials, and correspondence between AFRO publishers and civil rights leaders.
claims.evidence: Baltimore Beat (Aug 2026): 'Afro Charities, which manages AFRO Archives, a repository of more than a century of Black history in Baltimore and across the globe... The AFRO Archives holds a collection of thousands of original AFRO American newspapers, as well as more than 3 million photographs, rare audio/visual materials, and thousands of letters between publishers of the AFRO American and civil rights leaders.'
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source for the holdings figures; executive director Savannah Wood is the attributed source within the article.

claims.claim: In November 2007 a Mellon Foundation grant funded students from Johns Hopkins, Morgan State, and Goucher to inventory and describe the AFRO archives held at the newspaper's headquarters, with the goal of creating a searchable online database.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (citing contemporary reports): 'In November 2007, five students were selected from Baltimore institutions, Johns Hopkins University, Morgan State University and Goucher College, to begin work under an Andrew W. Mellon Foundation grant to uncover and describe the content of the newspaper's archives, held at its headquarters... ultimately create an online database for searching the material.' Johns Hopkins' own news release (July 2007) confirms the grant and practicum.
claims.uncertainty: Low on the grant and project; whether the online database was completed is not confirmed in these sources.

claims.claim: The AFRO remains led by 4th- and 5th-generation descendants of founder John H. Murphy Sr., and partners with Morgan State University's School of Global Journalism and Communication.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'Today, the AFRO is led by 4th and 5th generation descendants of John H. Murphy Sr. It is in partnership with the Strategic Communications and Journalism Departments of Morgan State University's School of Global Journalism and Communication.'
claims.uncertainty: Secondary source; family-ownership claim is longstanding and widely reported.

entities.name: Allen Media Group
entities.description: Black-owned media conglomerate founded by Byron Allen: broadcast TV affiliates, cable/digital networks (The Weather Channel, TheGrio), streaming platforms (Local Now), and syndicated programming.

claims.claim: Allen filed a $20 billion racial-discrimination suit against Comcast in February 2015 under Section 1981 of the Civil Rights Act of 1866, alleging refusal to carry his channels; the Supreme Court ruled 9-0 against him in March 2020 (but-for causation standard), and the parties settled in June 2020 with Comcast picking up Comedy.TV, Recipe.TV, and JusticeCentral.TV.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia Comcast v. NAAOM: suit filed Feb 2015 seeking $20B under Sec. 1981; SCOTUS unanimous March 2020 ruling; settlement after. Moguldom/Black Enterprise (June 2020): Comcast agreed to carry three channels (Comedy.TV, Recipe.TV, JusticeCentral.TV) and amended Weather Channel terms.
claims.source: Wikipedia: Comcast v. National Association of African-American-Owned Media; Moguldom/Black Enterprise
claims.uncertainty: Low

claims.claim: Allen also filed a $10 billion discrimination suit against Charter Communications, settled February 2021.
claims.evidence: Moguldom (2021): 'Byron Allen, Charter Communications Settle $10 Billion Racial Discrimination Suit — February 10, 2021' (headline-level).
claims.uncertainty: Headline-level evidence; settlement terms not documented in this pass.

claims.claim: Allen Media Group was founded by Byron Allen in 1993 and operates broadcast stations, cable/digital networks, and film/TV production.
claims.evidence: UrbanHollywood411 (2025): 'Allen Media Group operates under the leadership of chairman and CEO Byron Allen, who founded the company in 1993.'
claims.source: UrbanHollywood411, 'Layoffs Sweep Through Byron Allen's TheGrio'
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Allen acquired TheGrio in 2016 and grew it from under 1 million to a peak of 10.5 million monthly active users (company claim, 2020).
claims.evidence: HipHopWired (2020): Allen 'purchased the website in 2016 and successfully grew its active [users] from less than 1 million to an astounding 10.5 million active users.'
claims.source: HipHopWired, 'Byron Allen Announces The Grio.TV Is Launching MLK Weekend'
claims.uncertainty: Audience figure is a company claim (primary, self-interested), not independently verified.

claims.claim: In 2022 Allen bought the bankrupt Black News Channel's assets for a reported $11 million and merged them into TheGrio TV.
claims.evidence: US Times Mirror: 'purchased the assets of the Black News Channel out of bankruptcy for a reported $11 million, merging its TV assets and carriage deals into TheGrio's network.'
claims.source: US Times Mirror, 'How Byron Allen went from comic to media mogul'
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source for the $11M figure.

claims.claim: Allen Media Group was founded by Byron Allen in 1993 and is headquartered in Los Angeles with offices in New York and Atlanta.
claims.evidence: Company boilerplate in 2026 press materials and investor filings consistently state Allen founded the company in 1993.
claims.source: Allen Media Group press releases via PR Newswire, May-September 2026; BuzzFeed investor announcement
claims.uncertainty: Low; consistently reported across company and investor sources.

claims.claim: The company states it owns/operates 13 ABC-CBS-NBC network affiliate broadcast stations in 11 U.S. markets and ten 24-hour HD television networks (The Weather Channel, Pets.TV, Comedy.TV, Recipe.TV, Cars.TV, ES.TV, MyDestination.TV, JusticeCentral.TV, TheGrio Television Network, HBCU GO) serving nearly 315 million subscribers.
claims.contradictory: Wikipedia's Allen Media Group entry shows the broadcast stations as sold in 2026; company PR from September 2026 still claims ownership/operation of 13 affiliates.
claims.evidence: Company boilerplate in September 2026 press releases (DPAA summit keynote announcement).
claims.source: Allen Media Group press materials via PR Newswire, 2026-09
claims.uncertainty: Company-reported; subscriber figure is a gross-distribution claim, not measured audience.

claims.claim: In 2026, Byron Allen's family office acquired a majority of the outstanding shares of BuzzFeed, Inc., with Allen becoming Chairman and CEO.
claims.evidence: BuzzFeed investor announcement via Wedbush; confirmed in September 2026 Allen Media Group press boilerplate.
claims.source: BuzzFeed, Inc. investor announcement; Allen Media Group press materials
claims.uncertainty: Low; confirmed across investor and company channels.

claims.claim: In May 2026 Allen Media Group inked a new long-term portfolio carriage renewal with YouTube TV covering The Weather Channel, JusticeCentral, Comedy.TV, Recipe.TV, and its Local Now free-streaming platform.
claims.evidence: Company press release announcing the YouTube TV renewal.
claims.uncertainty: Low; first-party announcement of a carriage deal.

claims.claim: On June 14, 2016, Byron Allen's Entertainment Studios acquired TheGrio, which remained 100% African American-owned, and announced plans to expand it into a multi-platform network.
claims.evidence: Urban Intellectuals (PRNewswire release, June 14, 2016): 'Entertainment Studios... acquires the African American-targeted news network TheGrio... will remain 100% African American-owned.' Black Enterprise: Byron Allen acquired TheGrio from NBCUniversal and planned to turn it into 'a multi-platform network.'
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: Allen Media Group/Entertainment Studios pursued large-scale consolidation: it acquired the Weather Channel's TV assets for approximately $300 million in March 2018 and bid for BET Media Group in 2023.
claims.contradictory: Reported Allen bid for BET ranges from ~$2.7B to ~$3B across outlets; no official figure was disclosed.
claims.evidence: Good News Planet: Allen acquired 'The Weather Channel's TV assets for ~$300 million' (March 2018). ClutchPoints/LakersDaily: Allen's group pursued BET Media Group in 2023; Paramount declined.
claims.uncertainty: Deal figures are secondhand reporting; BET bid was not consummated.

entities.name: American Urban Radio Networks
entities.description: National Black-targeted radio network company formed from the SBN/NBN merger; owner now Access.1 Communications.

claims.claim: AURN was formed in 1991 from the merger of the Sheridan Broadcasting Network and the National Black Network.
claims.contradictory: National Black Network Wikipedia says 'By 1995.'
claims.evidence: AURN Wikipedia: 'formed in 1991 from a merger of the Sheridan Broadcasting Network (SBN) and National Black Network (NBN).'
claims.uncertainty: NBN's own Wikipedia article gives 'By 1995'; 1991 is the AURN article's date.

claims.claim: In May 2016, Access.1 Communications took 100% ownership of AURN.
claims.evidence: AURN Wikipedia and Alchetron: 'In May 2016 NBN parent company Access.1 Communications Corporation took over 100% ownership of American Urban Radio Networks.'
claims.uncertainty: Low on the fact of the transfer. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

claims.claim: AURN describes itself as the only African-American-owned-and-operated Nielsen RADAR-rated radio network; RBR reported that parent Access.1 is 'controlled by Guggenheim Capital Partners,' a non-Black firm — leaving AURN's effective Black ownership contested.
claims.contradictory: AURN's self-description as Black-owned vs RBR's claim Access.1 is controlled by Guggenheim Capital Partners.
claims.evidence: AURN Wikipedia/LinkedIn: 'only African-American-owned-and-operated Nielsen RADAR-rated radio network'; RBR+TVBR: 'Access.1 is controlled by Guggenheim Capital Partners.'
claims.uncertainty: Ownership layers (Access.1 vs Guggenheim) make 'Black-owned' status ambiguous; no FCC or primary filing reviewed to resolve.

entities.name: Amistad Research Center
entities.description: The nation's oldest and largest independent Black-history archive, at Tulane University in New Orleans; currently under severe financial strain from federal funding cuts.

claims.claim: The Amistad Research Center is an independent archive of Black history and culture based at Tulane University in New Orleans, on whose campus it has sat since 1987.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'The board voted to relocate to Tulane University, and the ARC has been on its campus in Uptown New Orleans since 1987.'
claims.uncertainty: Low. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

claims.claim: Holdings include approximately 800 manuscript collections, 250,000 photographs dating to 1860, about 14,000 reels of microfilm, and nearly 8,000 moving-image and sound-recording items, with papers of figures including W.E.B. Du Bois, Zora Neale Hurston, Fannie Lou Hamer, and Claude McKay.
claims.contradictory: A 2026 Baltimore Beat report describes '15 million Black history artifacts dating back to the 1780s'; a Google Arts & Culture exhibit cites 'over ten million documents.' Item-count methodologies differ across sources.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia holdings section: 'approximately 800 manuscript collections... 250,000 photographs dating from 1860... Microfilm holdings... total approximately 14,000 reels. The moving image and sound recordings holdings include nearly 8,000 items.'
claims.uncertainty: Counts vary by source and counting method; treat as order-of-magnitude.

claims.claim: In 2026 the Center laid off half its staff after federal funding cuts; roughly 40% of its annual budget had come from the federal government.
claims.evidence: Baltimore Beat (Aug 2026): 'The Amistad Research Center in New Orleans, which holds 15 million Black history artifacts dating back to the 1780s, has had to lay off half its staff due to federal funding cuts.' Afro Charities executive director Savannah Wood is quoted on the vulnerability of single-source funding: the Center 'had 40% of its annual budget coming from the federal government.'
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source; layoff figures not corroborated by a second outlet or the Center itself in this research.

entities.name: ANA Alliance for Inclusive and Multicultural Marketing (AIMM)
entities.description: Association of National Advertisers' multicultural marketing arm; commissions the benchmark studies documenting the gap between multicultural population share and multicultural ad spend.

claims.claim: A PQ Media study for ANA/AIMM (U.S. Multicultural Media Forecast 2019) found multicultural consumers were nearly 40% of the U.S. population but multicultural media was only 5.2% of total advertising/marketing spend: $25.9B total in 2018, with African-American media at $7.2B (+6.1% YoY).
claims.evidence: PRODU and AListDaily (via anaaimm.net) reporting on the study.
claims.uncertainty: Industry-commissioned research; figures are reported, not independently verified. One outlet's reprint appears to typo African-American media as '$7.2 million' vs '$7.2 billion.'

claims.claim: AIMM reported that investment in diverse-owned media by the largest media holding companies was 2.5% in 2023 ($1.9B), up from 2.2% in 2022 — far below population-representative levels.
claims.evidence: Nielsen/Gracenote 2024 Inclusive Ad Spend report citing AIMM research with MAVEN and Media Framework (formerly Standard Media Index).
claims.uncertainty: Industry-reported; methodology covers only the largest media holding companies.

entities.name: Angelica Nwandu
entities.description: Founder and CEO of The Shade Room; built the largest Instagram-native Black media brand from a personal account.

claims.claim: Angelica Nwandu founded The Shade Room in March 2014, building it as an Instagram-based media company; Forbes named her to its 30 Under 30 list in 2016.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'founded by Angelica Nwandu in March 2014'; AllAmericanSpeakers bio: 'In 2016, Forbes named Nwandu to its 30 Under 30 list, saying she 'revolutionized celebrity gossip'.'
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Nwandu bootstrapped The Shade Room with a single VC investment, growing it to 100K followers within weeks and later 24M+; she chose Instagram because she 'personally could not build a website.'
claims.evidence: Africa Summit bio: 'With a single VC investment, she bootstrapped TSR, which she grew to 100K followers ('Roommates') within weeks... Nwandu turned to Instagram to launch TSR because she personally could not build a website.'
claims.uncertainty: Founder-narrative sourcing (self-interested) for the origin story; growth figures approximate.

entities.name: Apple App Tracking Transparency
entities.description: Apple's 2021 privacy framework limiting cross-app ad tracking; flagged as a platform risk but not verified against Black publishers in this pass.

claims.claim: Apple rolled out App Tracking Transparency (ATT) in 2021, requiring opt-in for cross-app tracking (IDFA), which reduced ad targeting and monetization for app- and social-dependent publishers.
claims.evidence: No source captured in this research pass; widely reported in trade press but not verified here.
claims.uncertainty: HIGH: included because the track brief names Apple privacy changes as a theme, but no verified source was captured and no Black-publisher-specific impact was documented. Verify before use.

entities.name: Aspire TV
entities.description: Black-targeted cable network launched by Magic Johnson in 2012; now under UP Entertainment.

claims.claim: Aspire TV was launched by Magic Johnson (with Comcast and GMC/Up TV) in June 2012 as part of Comcast's commitment — a condition of the FCC/DOJ approval of the NBCUniversal deal — to carry minority-owned independent networks; it promised 'positive, uplifting images of African Americans.'
claims.contradictory: Launch day reported as June 27, 2012 (Wikipedia, Alchetron) vs 'June 30' (ESPN/AP, Feb 2012).
claims.evidence: ESPN/AP (Feb 2012): Johnson launching Aspire; 'Comcast Corp. reached an agreement with the FCC and Department of Justice to diversify' — network to launch June 30. Comcast (Feb 2012; 2014): Aspire among four minority-owned networks selected; partnership with Magic Johnson and GMC TV. Alchetron/Wikipedia: launched June 27, 2012.
claims.source: ESPN/AP; Comcast corporate; Wikipedia: Aspire TV
claims.uncertainty: Exact launch day disputed (June 27 vs June 30, 2012); commitment context well documented.

claims.claim: Magic Johnson divested his majority ownership of Aspire; it is now owned by UP Entertainment (under SVP Angela Cannon), which also launched AspireTV+ on Prime Video Channels in 2024.
claims.contradictory: Wikipedia text says 'In 2019, Johnson divested his majority ownership after 10 year' — arithmetic is inconsistent with a 2012 launch (10 years = ~2022), so the reported year is suspect.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia Aspire TV: 'aspireTV is now owned by UP Entertainment under the leadership of Senior VP of Multicultural Networks and Strategy Angela Cannon'; AspireTV+ launched 2024 on Prime Video.
claims.uncertainty: Ownership transfer to UP Entertainment verified; the year of divestiture is internally inconsistent in the source — mark date Unresolved.

entities.name: Associated Negro Press
entities.description: First national news service for African-American newspapers, founded 1919 in Chicago by Claude Barnett; supplied twice-weekly news packets to ~150 US Black papers plus ~100 in Africa; ceased in the 1960s.

claims.claim: Founded March 2, 1919 in Chicago by Claude Albert Barnett; the first (and later largest) national news service serving African-American newspapers - the Black press's equivalent of the Associated Press.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (founding date, founder) and Nieman Reports ("first (and later largest) national news service") agree.
claims.source: Wikipedia (Associated Negro Press); Nieman Reports timeline
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: The ANP supplied news stories, columns, features, reviews and photos in twice-weekly packets (by mail, later more frequent), serving about 150 US Black newspapers and about 100 newspapers in Africa, plus the West Indies after WWII.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (150 US + 100 Africa); Claude Barnett Wikipedia (200 papers in 1950, incl. West Indies/Africa).
claims.source: Wikipedia (Associated Negro Press; Claude Albert Barnett)
claims.uncertainty: Medium: service counts vary by year and source (150 vs 200 vs 225).
claims.contradictory: ~150 US papers (ANP article) vs 200 papers in 1950 (Barnett article) vs 225 subscribers by 1935 (America Comes Alive).

claims.claim: Barnett built the ANP into an international network crusading against Jim Crow and colonialism, and during WWII he and other Black journalists pressured the US government to accredit Black war correspondents.
claims.evidence: Nieman Reports on the international anti-Jim-Crow/colonialism crusade; African American Registry and Wikipedia on the WWII accreditation pressure.
claims.source: Nieman Reports; African American Registry; Wikipedia (Claude Albert Barnett)
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: The ANP ceased operating in the mid-1960s - Wikipedia lists it as defunct in 1964, while the African American Registry says it ceased after Barnett's 1967 death.
claims.evidence: Direct conflict between the two sources.
claims.source: Wikipedia (Associated Negro Press); African American Registry
claims.uncertainty: High: end date disputed.
claims.contradictory: Defunct 1964 (Wikipedia) vs ceased after Barnett's death in 1967 (African American Registry).

entities.name: Atlanta Black Star
entities.description: Digital-first news publication focused on the African American perspective on politics; self-described as the largest Black-owned digital publication in the US.

claims.claim: Atlanta Black Star was founded in 2012 by Neil 'Jelani' Nelson, Tracy Dornelly, and Andre Moore; it is owned by Diamond Diaspora Media and based in Atlanta.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'It was founded in 2012 by Neil 'Jelani' Nelson, Tracy Dornelly, and Andre Moore.'; owner listed as Diamond Diaspora Media.
claims.uncertainty: Low. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

claims.claim: The site self-reports over 14 million monthly unique visitors and participates in a Facebook partnership program.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'The site has over 14 million monthly unique visitors'; 'The site is part of a partnership program with Facebook.'
claims.uncertainty: Visitor figure is self-reported; partnership-program detail is thinly sourced. comScore 2023 put atlantablackstar.com at 5.9M uniques, down 16.1% (Journal-isms).

claims.claim: Its reporting has been republished or cited by Yahoo News, The Washington Post, and The New York Times.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'Media outlets such as Yahoo News, The Washington Post, The New York Times, Heavy.com, and The Daily Dot have republished or cited the contents of the Atlanta Black Star.'
claims.uncertainty: Single tertiary source.

entities.name: Atlanta Daily World
entities.description: Founded 1928 in Atlanta; the first successful African-American daily newspaper in the US; now owned by Real Times Inc. and publishing daily online.

claims.claim: Founded as the weekly Atlanta World on August 5, 1928 by 26-year-old Morehouse graduate William Alexander Scott II.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia, BlackPast, and BET agree on Aug 5, 1928 founding and Scott's age/education.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: The paper became a daily on March 13, 1932 (per BET and BlackPast), becoming the first successful African-American daily newspaper in US history; Wikipedia says it became a daily in 1931.
claims.evidence: BET "This Day in Black History" and BlackPast cite March 13, 1932; Wikipedia text says daily in 1931.
claims.uncertainty: Medium: year differs between sources (1931 vs 1932).
claims.contradictory: Daily conversion 1931 (Wikipedia) vs March 13, 1932 (BET, BlackPast).

claims.claim: Scott built the first chain of Black newspapers (Chattanooga Tribune and Memphis World in 1931, growing into the Scott Newspaper Syndicate, later described as reaching 50 publications at peak by some sources and over 240 associated papers by historian Thomas Aiello).
claims.evidence: BlackPast/Wikipedia: chain of fifty; Aiello's "The Grapevine of the Black South" (UGA Press, 2018): more than 240 papers associated at peak.
claims.source: BlackPast.org; New Books Network podcast on Aiello's book, 2019-09-19
claims.uncertainty: High: peak scale figures differ sharply (50 vs 240+) depending on how "associated" is counted.
claims.contradictory: 50 publications (BlackPast/Wikipedia) vs 240+ (Aiello).

claims.claim: Scott was shot and killed outside his home in 1934 at age 32; no one was ever convicted.
claims.evidence: BlackPast account of the unsolved 1934 murder.
claims.uncertainty: Low for the fact of the murder; motive unproven.

claims.claim: In 1944 reporter Harry McAlpin became the first Black reporter to cover a presidential press conference (Roosevelt, then Truman White House).
claims.evidence: Nieman Reports timeline entry.
claims.source: Nieman Reports, "Timeline: Milestones of the Black Press in the U.S."
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: The paper is currently owned by Real Times Inc. and publishes daily online.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia infobox: owner Real Times Inc., "publishes daily online."
claims.uncertainty: Low. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

entities.name: Audacy, Inc.
entities.description: Second-largest U.S. radio owner; programs urban formats (including acquired heritage urban brands) while its senior decision-making remains non-Black — Black-TARGETED under non-Black ownership.

claims.claim: Audacy (formerly Entercom, after the 2017 CBS Radio merger) acquired the WAMO urban format in Pittsburgh from Martz Communications Group and programs urban leaders such as KTWV-FM (The Wave) in Los Angeles.
claims.evidence: Radio Online industry report on the WAMO deal; Radio Facts ratings commentary on KTWV.
claims.uncertainty: Low for the WAMO acquisition; general urban-format footprint reported across outlets.

claims.claim: Industry commentary notes that while Radio One/Urban One remains the largest Black-owned radio company, senior decision-making at iHeartMedia and Audacy is not representative of the urban audiences they serve.
claims.evidence: Radio Facts analysis of ownership vs. decision-making in urban radio.
claims.uncertainty: Analytical claim by a trade commentator, not a demographic audit.

entities.name: Baltimore Afro-American (AFRO)
entities.description: Baltimore weekly founded 1892; the longest-running African-American family-owned newspaper in the US, still led by founder John H. Murphy Sr.'s descendants.

claims.claim: The paper traces to the Home Protector (1889); it became the Afro-American on August 13, 1892, and in 1897 John H. Murphy Sr. - born into slavery, a Civil War veteran - bought the printing equipment for $200 borrowed from his wife Martha; the Murphy family has owned it ever since, making it the longest-running African-American family-owned newspaper in the US.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia and NNPA recount the 1892 founding, the $200 purchase from wife Martha Howard Murphy, and continuous family ownership.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Under Carl Murphy (editor-publisher for 45 years after 1922), the AFRO expanded to as many as 13 national editions and peak circulation over 225,000, competing with the Chicago Defender and Pittsburgh Courier for the largest Black paper in America.
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia.com: 13 editions "between the two world wars", circulation "reached over 225,000"; African American Registry: "most widely circulated Black paper on the Atlantic coast" by 1922.
claims.uncertainty: Medium: peak circulation figure from secondary encyclopedia entry, not audited.

claims.claim: The AFRO launched the "Clean Block" campaign in the 1930s (still operating), campaigned against Jim Crow railroad cars and for equal pay for Maryland's Black teachers, and stationed correspondents in Europe, the Pacific, Africa and Japan during World War II.
claims.evidence: African American Registry details the campaigns and wartime correspondents; Edinburgh University library blog confirms Clean Block and wartime coverage.
claims.source: African American Registry; University of Edinburgh HCA Librarian blog, 2019
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Today the paper operates as AFRO News with Baltimore and Washington, D.C. offices, led by Dr. Frances "Toni" Draper, the founder's great-granddaughter, as CEO/publisher and board chair; succession planning is an active concern.
claims.evidence: NNPA 2024 article quotes Draper and describes the current structure and succession question.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Beck Cultural Exchange Center
entities.description: Knoxville's Black history museum/center, preserving Tennessee Black newspapers since the 1970s; the site of documented evidence that some Black papers survive nowhere at all.

claims.claim: The Beck Cultural Exchange Center in Knoxville has been collecting and preserving historic Black newspapers since the 1970s.
claims.evidence: Knox News (Jan 27, 2026): 'Beck has been collecting and preserving Black newspapers in Tennessee since the 1970s.'
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: KNOWN LOSS: Some historic Tennessee Black newspapers have no extant archived copies at all, according to a UT professor's spreadsheet research; ephemeral paper stock and historically white-biased collecting institutions are the cited causes.
claims.evidence: Knox News (2026): UT professor's research into Tennessee's Black newspapers found that some titles have no surviving archived copies. 'These newspapers were printed on cheap paper that wasn't made to last. And the institutions that could have saved them often focused on white history, leaving Black stories undocumented.'
claims.uncertainty: The specific titles and their counts were not itemized in this report; treat title-level detail as unresolved.

claims.claim: Knox News's 2026 reporting treats the digitization of Beck's collection as an open preservation gap: the paper stock is deteriorating and access remains largely analog.
claims.evidence: Knox News (2026) frames the story as an active preservation crisis: cheap newsprint deteriorating, with digitization and broader archiving still needed.
claims.uncertainty: Report's framing; specific digitization timelines not given.

entities.name: BET (Black Entertainment Television)
entities.description: Flagship Black-targeted television brand founded 1980 by Robert L. Johnson; Black-owned until its sale to Viacom in 2000. Includes BET, BET Her, BET Gospel, BET Jams, BET Soul, BET Studios, BET+, and VH1.

claims.claim: BET launched January 25, 1980, as a two-hour weekly programming block on the Madison Square Garden Sports Network (which became USA Network three months later), consisting of music videos and reruns of Black sitcoms.
claims.evidence: BET launched as a USA Network programming block on January 25, 1980, originally broadcasting two hours a week; the host network was the Madison Square Garden Sports Network, renamed USA Network three months after BET launched.
claims.source: Wikipedia: BET (television); African American Registry (Jan 25, 1980 entry)
claims.uncertainty: Low

claims.claim: BET became a full-time standalone cable channel in 1982/1983, evolving from the programming block.
claims.contradictory: Wikipedia says full-fledged channel in September 1982; African American Registry says 'it would not be until 1983 that BET became a full-fledged entity, independent of any other channel or programming block'; Simple Wikipedia also says 1983.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (BET television) states BET evolved into a full-fledged cable channel in September 1982; aaregistry.org says 1983.
claims.uncertainty: Exact month of full-time launch uncertain: Sept 1982 vs 1983.

claims.claim: BET became the first Black-controlled company listed on the New York Stock Exchange in 1991.
claims.evidence: In 1991, the network became the first Black-controlled company on the New York Stock Exchange (per liquisearch history; Black Enterprise notes it as an early-1990s milestone).
claims.source: liquisearch.com Black Entertainment Television - History; Black Enterprise (BET sale discussions article)
claims.uncertainty: Low

claims.claim: BET ceased to be Black-owned when sold to Viacom; as of 2026 it sits in Paramount Skydance's Media Networks division under the BET Media Group, and its US pay-TV reach fell from a 2011 peak of ~92M households to ~67M (Nov 2023).
claims.evidence: 'In 2003, the network was no longer a black owned business when it was bought by media conglomerate Viacom' (liquisearch); Wikipedia lists owner Paramount Media Networks / parent BET Media Group; carriage ~67M Nov 2023 vs 92M peak 2011.
claims.uncertainty: Low

claims.claim: BET launched in 1980 under founder Robert L. Johnson as the first Black-owned cable network; its 1991 IPO made it the first Black-controlled company listed on the New York Stock Exchange.
claims.evidence: BET.com: 'BET hit the air in 1980... Under founder Bob Johnson, BET grew from a 2-hour, Friday-night cable television network to a Black culture juggernaut.' Black Enterprise: 'With an initial public offering in 1991, BET became the first Black-controlled company to be listed on the New York Stock Exchange.'
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: In 2001 BET Holdings was acquired by Viacom for approximately $3 billion, making Johnson the first Black billionaire; the sale ended Black ownership of the network.
claims.contradictory: Most sources say ~$3 billion; some contemporaneous reports say $2.9 billion. The discrepancy is rounding.
claims.evidence: Black Enterprise: 'In 2001, BET was acquired by Viacom for approximately $3 billion, making Johnson the first Black billionaire.'
claims.uncertainty: None material on the ownership transition.

claims.claim: In April 2016 BET acquired the Soul Train brand and media library — more than 1,100 TV episodes and 40 specials — from InterMedia Partners and Yucaipa Companies.
claims.evidence: BET.com: 'BET Networks... announced today that it has acquired the iconic SOUL TRAIN brand and library from InterMedia Partners and Yucaipa Companies. The deal includes more than 1,100 episodes and 40 specials from the 1970s through the first decade of the 2000s.' The Wrap: deal closed April 4, 2016.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: In 2023 Paramount explored selling BET Media Group; the process ended in August 2023 without a deal, keeping BET under Paramount ownership. Reported bidders included Tyler Perry (~$2 billion bid) and Byron Allen.
claims.evidence: ClutchPoints (2023): 'Paramount Ends Process To Sell BET Media Group, Keeps It In Its Stable... sale talks included media mogul Tyler Perry... a $2 billion bid to purchase BET from Paramount Global.' AfroTech: Byron Allen's Entertainment Studios also pursued BET.
claims.uncertainty: Bid amounts are secondhand reporting; no deal terms were officially disclosed.

claims.claim: BET was founded in 1980 by Robert L. Johnson (with Sheila Johnson) and in 1991 became the first Black-owned company listed on the New York Stock Exchange.
claims.evidence: TheWrap and Black media histories; blksociety.com retrospective.
claims.uncertainty: Low for founding; the NYSE 'first' claim is widely repeated but sourced here to secondary outlets.

claims.claim: Viacom acquired BET in 2000; reported deal values conflict — $2.3 billion per EURweb and other outlets, versus 'roughly $3 billion' per blksociety.com (which also dates the close to 2001).
claims.contradictory: Two cited sources disagree on both value and year; contemporaneous deal reporting needed to resolve.
claims.evidence: EURweb (2025) reports $2.3B/2000; blksociety.com (2026) reports ~$3B/2001.
claims.uncertainty: Material disagreement on price ($2.3B vs ~$3B) and closing year (2000 vs 2001) between secondary sources.

claims.claim: Paramount repeatedly explored selling BET (pausing talks in August 2023 after interest from Tyler Perry, Byron Allen, and Group Black; reported $1.6-1.7B talks with BET CEO Scott Mills' investor group in July 2024), but in August 2025 new Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison confirmed BET is not for sale and is central to the company's streaming strategy.
claims.evidence: TheWrap, Black Enterprise, Hot97, Wikipedia, EURweb.
claims.uncertainty: Low for Ellison's statement; the 2024 Mills talks were reported (Bloomberg via outlets), not confirmed by the companies.

claims.claim: BET remains Black-TARGETED but not Black-OWNED: it has been controlled by Viacom/Paramount entities since 2000, and Black-led bids to return it to Black ownership (Perry, Allen, Mills-led group) were not consummated.
claims.evidence: Sale history and August 2025 decision to keep BET within Paramount Skydance.
claims.uncertainty: Low; ownership chain is consistent across sources.

entities.name: BET programming debates
entities.description: The long-running two-sided debate over BET's programming quality and cultural responsibility.

claims.claim: Critics argued BET programming promoted negative stereotypes: in the mid-2000s community leaders protested misogynistic rap-video content and shows like 'Hot Ghetto Mess'; in 2007 Rev. Delman Coates led ~500 protesters to Debra Lee's home, launching the 'Enough is Enough' campaign.
claims.evidence: Refinery29 (2018): community leaders spoke out against negative stereotypes BET perpetuated with shows like Hot Ghetto Mess plus misogynistic messages in rap videos; in 2007 a Maryland reverend led 500 protesters to Lee's home in Washington DC, returning weekly. Essence interview with Coates (Enough is Enough) documents sustained meetings with BET leadership.
claims.source: Refinery29 (Debra Lee profile, 2018); Essence ('Fight BET' interview with Delman Coates)
claims.uncertainty: Low

claims.claim: Hampton University president William R. Harvey criticized BET's 2017 HBCU-set drama 'The Quad' as 'a sad, derisive and degenerating story' and 'an incredibly disparaging depiction of the HBCUs I know and love.'
claims.evidence: EURweb/Ebony (2017): Harvey sent Debra Lee a scathing letter calling The Quad 'a sad, derisive and degenerating story,' arguing it feeds a false narrative about the irrelevance of HBCUs.
claims.uncertainty: Low

claims.claim: The Adult Swim satire 'The Boondocks' aired a 2008 episode parodying BET executives Debra Lee and Reginald Hudlin, accusing the network of recycling 's***ty' MTV reality shows into Black versions.
claims.evidence: 2008 episode of The Boondocks (Aaron McGruder) caricatured 'Dr. Leevil' (Lee) and 'Weggie Rudlin' (Reginald Hudlin) planning 'a hoe-wards show' — widely reported in press at the time.
claims.uncertainty: Episode parody documented via fan/livejournal coverage; contemporaneous press verification not re-confirmed in this pass.

claims.claim: Defenders, including Debra Lee herself, framed BET's role as serving a diverse Black audience: Lee's stated brand filter was 'respect, reflect and elevate' — programming must 'have a message, can't be derogatory and has to show positive images' — and she argued 'The Black audience is not monolithic.'
claims.evidence: BET.com/Forbes interview: Lee said 'Our programming filter now is: It has to have a message, can't be derogatory and has to show positive images... We respect, reflect and elevate our audience.' AfroTech (2025): Lee defended the value of Black programming against recent cancellations, citing audience demand.
claims.uncertainty: Low

entities.name: BET sale attempt (2023)
entities.description: Paramount's aborted 2023 sale of BET Media Group and the bidder field.

claims.claim: Paramount Global explored selling a majority stake in BET Media Group in March 2023; reported bidders included Tyler Perry (~$2B, backed by Ariel Alternatives), Byron Allen (~$2.7B-$3B), Sean Combs, Group Black, 50 Cent, Kenya Barris, and Shaquille O'Neal.
claims.contradictory: Bid figures come from press leaks (NY Post via clutchpoints/eurweb): Perry ~$2B, Allen ~$2.7B; Paramount's ask was ~$3B (10x EBITDA vs bids at ~8x). Exact terms never confirmed by Paramount.
claims.evidence: TheWrap (Aug 2023): bidders included Perry and Allen plus Shaq/Group Black, 50 Cent, Kenya Barris. Clutchpoints/NY Post: Paramount wanted $3B; Perry offered $2B; Allen offered $2.7B.
claims.uncertainty: Leaked bid figures, never officially confirmed; treat as provisional.

claims.claim: On August 16, 2023 Paramount cancelled the sale, telling bidders a sale 'wouldn't result in any meaningful deleveraging of its balance sheet'; Perry called the process 'disrespectful' and said he would not overpay; BET remained Paramount-owned.
claims.evidence: WSJ (via TheWrap, Essence, eurweb): Paramount informed bidders Aug 16, 2023 the sale was off. Moguldom (Oct 2023): Perry said at Bloomberg Equality Summit, 'The way it happened was disrespectful in a lot of ways' and 'Don't try to get me to pay for something that's not worth anywhere near the value.'
claims.source: Wall Street Journal via TheWrap/Essence; Moguldom (Perry quotes)
claims.uncertainty: Low

claims.claim: BET+ (launched 2019) counts Tyler Perry as a minority investor (reported 25% stake); BET Studios (2021) counts Kenya Barris and Rashida Jones as stakeholders — complicating any future sale.
claims.evidence: THR via radiox (2023): 'BET+, for example, counts Tyler Perry as an investor, while BET Studios counts Kenya Barris and Rashida Jones as stakeholders.' popculture (2023): Perry 'currently owns a 25% stake in BET's streaming service.' Adweek (2021): BET+ rolled out Sept 2019.
claims.uncertainty: 25% figure from single secondary source; launch month (Sept 2019 vs June) varies by outlet.

entities.name: Black Classic Press
entities.description: Baltimore-based independent Black book publisher founded 1978 by W. Paul Coates; reprints out-of-print works by/about people of African descent; runs BCP Digital Printing (1995).

claims.claim: Founded in 1978 in Baltimore, Maryland by W. Paul Coates (father of Ta-Nehisi Coates), originally working from his basement; mission is to publish obscure and significant books by and about people of African descent, mostly out-of-print historical works brought back into print (~6 titles/year).
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (1978, Coates, basement, mission, ~6 titles/year); Publishers Weekly confirms.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: BCP Digital Printing, launched in 1995, is the company's short-run book-printing arm - described by Coates as possibly the only full-time African-American book printer in the US - and accounts for about 85% of company revenue; Coates says the publishing side would have folded without it.
claims.evidence: Publishers Weekly 2015 interview with Coates (1995 launch, 85% revenue share, "only Black book printer" quote, total sales approaching $2M).
claims.uncertainty: Medium: "only Black book printer" is Coates' own claim after 20 years of looking; revenue figures self-reported.

claims.claim: BCP grew out of Coates' George Jackson Prison Movement (1972 prison-literacy program) and The Black Book bookstore, influenced by Lewis Michaux's African National Memorial Bookstore in Harlem; since 2015 it has acquired backlist titles from Carter Woodson's Associated Publishers and Tony Martin's Majority Press.
claims.evidence: Publishers Weekly (2024 Literarian coverage; 2020 WI15 interview) details the prison-movement/bookstore origins, Michaux influence, and the Associated Publishers/Majority Press acquisitions.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: W. Paul Coates received the National Book Foundation's 2024 Literarian Award for Outstanding Service to the American Literary Community (presented by his son Ta-Nehisi Coates at the Nov 20, 2024 National Book Awards).
claims.evidence: Publishers Weekly announcement.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Black Enterprise
entities.description: Business magazine founded 1970 by Earl G. Graves Sr.; the first magazine devoted to Black entrepreneurship; diversified into a multimedia company with the annual BE 100s rankings.

claims.claim: Founded in 1970 by Earl G. Graves Sr.; the first issue (August 1970) featured Charles Evers on the cover; it was the first magazine dedicated to the advancement of African Americans through entrepreneurship, financial literacy and career development.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (1970, first-issue cover); Black Enterprise's own 40th-anniversary Titans list confirms August 1970 founding.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: The BE 100s - the annual ranking of the nation's largest Black-owned businesses - was first compiled and published in 1973.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia.
claims.uncertainty: Low. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

claims.claim: The magazine became profitable early - Wikipedia says since its 10th issue; Black Enterprise's own tribute says by its ninth issue - after Graves secured national advertisers such as PepsiCo and General Motors.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (10th issue) vs BlackEnterprise.com tribute (ninth issue); both agree on early profitability and the PepsiCo/GM ad wins.
claims.uncertainty: Medium: ninth vs tenth issue discrepancy.
claims.contradictory: Profitable since 9th issue (BE tribute) vs 10th issue (Wikipedia).

claims.claim: Black Enterprise grew into a diversified multimedia company (print, digital, broadcast, live events) with claimed readership of 3.7-6 million; Earl "Butch" Graves Jr. became CEO in 2006; Graves Sr. died April 6, 2020 at 85; the company reported $22 million revenue in 2017.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (58 employees, $22M 2017 revenue, 534,752 circulation 2013, Butch CEO 2006); Congressional Record tribute (April 6, 2020 death); BE obituary.
claims.uncertainty: Medium: readership/revenue figures are company-reported.

claims.claim: Black Enterprise was founded in 1970 by Earl G. Graves Sr. and has been Black-owned since; it launched blackenterprise.com (originally BE Online) in 1997 and evolved into a digital-first multimedia/events company.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'The company was founded in 1970 by Earl G. Graves Sr.'; blackenterprise.com (50th anniversary): 'in 1997, BE went digital with BlackEnterprise.com (originally called BE Online).'
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Black Enterprise'; Black Enterprise, 'BLACK ENTERPRISE Turns 55 Years Old'
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Under CEO Earl 'Butch' Graves Jr., the company expanded from a single magazine into digital, video, podcasts, social, email, and live/virtual events reaching 6M+ African Americans.
claims.evidence: Black Enterprise: 'What began as a magazine in 1970 has evolved into a comprehensive multimedia platform, offering digital content on BlackEnterprise.com, engaging video productions, insightful podcasts, a vibrant social media presence, targeted email dispatches, and impactful live and virtual convenings.'
claims.source: Black Enterprise, 'Elevating Your Excellence: Earl 'Butch' Graves Jr. Leads Black Enterprise's 55-Year Charge'
claims.uncertainty: Company-published (primary, self-interested) for reach claims.

claims.claim: BlackEnterprise.com grew from under 1M monthly uniques (2019) to 6.5M (June 2022, Comscore), hiring 10+ writers, partly on 2020-era advertiser diversity pledges.
claims.evidence: Digiday (2022): 'Black Enterprise's traffic has grown from less than a million monthly uniques when Barton joined the company in 2019, to 6.5 million unique visitors in June 2022, according to Comscore data.'
claims.uncertainty: Comscore panel methodology; the Digiday piece itself notes the growth came from both pledges and the company's own audience work.

claims.claim: Black Enterprise was founded in August 1970 by Earl G. Graves Sr. and remains Black-owned under CEO Earl 'Butch' Graves Jr. (CEO since 2006), with Graves family leadership continuing after the founder's death in April 2020.
claims.evidence: Company's own anniversary coverage; HipHopWired obituary reporting; Howard University News Service.
claims.uncertainty: Low; founding date, succession and founder's death consistently reported.

claims.claim: The brand transitioned from a monthly print magazine to a digital-first multimedia platform (digital content, video, podcasts, events); the company's own anniversary coverage refers to the 50th-anniversary issue as 'the last regular print magazine.'
claims.evidence: BE's 55th-anniversary tribute coverage on blackenterprise.com.
claims.uncertainty: Medium; inference from the company's own phrasing about the print edition's end; exact final print date not stated in the source.

claims.claim: For decades BE published the BE 100s lists (largest Black-owned companies; advertising agencies), which served as an industry barometer of Black business development — the ad-agency list shrank from 20 firms/$798M in billings in 1998 to eight firms in 2016, its last year.
claims.evidence: Black Enterprise retrospective on the BE 100s ad-agency lists.
claims.uncertainty: Low for the figures as reported by BE; they are company-reported historical data.

entities.name: Black Journal / Tony Brown's Journal
entities.description: First nationally televised public-affairs program produced for, about, and by Black Americans.

claims.claim: Black Journal premiered June 12, 1968 on National Educational Television (NET) as a public-affairs series 'for blacks, about blacks' created after the 1967 urban uprisings; under executive producer William Greaves it won an Emmy in 1969.
claims.evidence: Thirteen/WNET (2020): premiered June 12, 1968 on NET; first episode included Coretta Scott King. wearespeaking.net: created in aftermath of 1967 uprisings; won an Emmy in 1969 under William Greaves.
claims.uncertainty: Low

claims.claim: Journalist Tony Brown took over in 1971; as stations grew uneasy, he moved it to commercial TV in 1977 with Pepsi sponsorship as 'Tony Brown's Journal'; it returned to PBS in 1982 and ran until 2008.
claims.evidence: wearespeaking.net: Brown exec producer/host by 1971; moved to commercial TV in 1977 with Pepsi sponsorship renamed Tony Brown's Journal; returned to PBS in 1982; ran until 2008. Wikipedia: NET 1968-1970, PBS 1970-1977; later commercial as Tony Brown's Journal; returned to public TV 1982; aired until 2008.
claims.uncertainty: Low

claims.claim: 59 episodes from 1968-1977 were digitized and released to stream free via the American Archive of Public Broadcasting in 2020.
claims.evidence: Library Journal infoDOCKET (2020): AAPB released 59 digitized episodes, largely unseen since airing 1968-1977.
claims.uncertainty: Low

entities.name: Black Press Archives, Moorland-Spingarn Research Center (Howard University)
entities.description: Howard University's Moorland-Spingarn Research Center newspaper collection: 2,000+ Black newspaper titles on microfilm, founded jointly with the NNPA in 1973 and now being digitized.

claims.claim: The Black Press Archives began in 1973 as a joint project of Howard University and the National Newspaper Publishers Association (NNPA), housed at Howard's Moorland-Spingarn Research Center.
claims.evidence: Howard MSRC's own page: 'The Black Press Archives began as a joint project of Howard University and the National Newspapers Publishers Association (NNPA) in 1973.' Corroborated by the Greene County Democrat (2017).
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: The collection represents more than 2,000 newspaper titles from the United States, Africa, and the African diaspora, comprising 2,847 microfilm reels and over 100,000 individual issues, plus complete files of Black papers and records of Black editors, publishers, and journalists.
claims.evidence: Howard MSRC: 'The Black Press Archives represents more than 2,000 newspaper titles from the United States, Africa and the African diaspora. It has 2,847 microfilm reels of newspapers, totaling over 100,000 individual issues of newspapers. The collection includes complete files of Black papers as well as the records of Black editors, publishers and journalists.'
claims.uncertainty: None material; holding institution's own description.

claims.claim: In February 2022 Howard's MSRC received a $2 million grant from the Jonathan Logan Family Foundation, in partnership with Howard's Center for Journalism and Democracy, to preserve and digitize the Black Press Archives for a worldwide online repository.
claims.evidence: Howard's The Dig (Feb 2022): 'The Howard University Moorland-Spingarn Research Center (MSRC) received a $2 million grant from the Jonathan Logan Family Foundation to support the preservation and digitization of the Black Press Archives... MSRC worked in partnership with the Center for Journalism and Democracy.' NNPA reported MSRC director Benjamin Talton's claim it would become 'the largest, most diverse, and the world's most accessible Black newspaper database.'
claims.uncertainty: Digitization is in progress; the 'largest/most accessible' characterization is an institutional aspiration, not a measured outcome.

claims.claim: Access for researchers is by appointment; the MSRC provides a research-appointment request process and email reference.
claims.evidence: MSRC Black Press Archives page: 'Make a Research Appointment' with reference email info@msrc-howard.libanswers.com.
claims.uncertainty: None.

entities.name: Black Star Network
entities.description: Free Black-owned streaming (OTT) network founded by Roland Martin in 2021, built around his daily #RolandMartinUnfiltered show and funded by donors and ads.

claims.claim: Black Star Network launched September 2, 2021, founded by journalist Roland Martin as a free, ad-supported OTT network (apps, Roku, AppleTV, FireTV, Samsung, Xbox) carrying Black news, politics, technology, and culture; described as 100% Black-owned.
claims.evidence: Final Call/NNPA (2021): Martin 'announced an over-the-top media (or OTT) network that will broadcast directly to viewers free via the internet and a phone app... Unlike several other Black content related news and information platforms, Black Star Network is 100 percent Black-owned.'; AfroTech confirms free, ad-supported model.
claims.source: Final Call News, 'Roland Martin announces New Black TV network'; AfroTech (2021)
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: The network grew out of #RolandMartinUnfiltered, a daily digital show (launched ~2018, per the third-anniversary timing) that the company says generated hundreds of millions of views.
claims.evidence: Final Call (2021): Martin announced the network 'on the third anniversary of #RolandMartinUnfiltered... averaging 20 to 30 million views a month'; AfroTech: the show 'generated nearly 509 million views and more than 1.5 billion minutes watched,' per a press release.
claims.source: Final Call News; AfroTech, 'Journalist Roland Martin Launches Free Streaming Network'
claims.uncertainty: View counts are company/press-release claims (primary, self-interested); show launch year derived from anniversary timing.

claims.claim: Martin funds the network through a donor/community model (asking supporters for ~$50/year) plus advertising, deliberately keeping it free because 'a lot of our people simply cannot afford to pay for a streaming service.'
claims.evidence: EURweb (2026): 'He has built his network on a donor-supported model rather than subscriptions, and he is asking supporters to contribute an average of $50 a year.'; Final Call (2021): 'The network will be ad supported.'
claims.source: EURweb, 'Roland Martin: Black-Owned Media Is Fighting for Its Life'; Final Call News
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Black-owned local TV stations
entities.description: The collapse and partial rebound of Black full-power broadcast-station ownership.

claims.claim: Free Press found 18 Black-owned and operated full-power commercial TV stations in 2006 (1.3%); by December 2012 only five remained; after Roberts Broadcasting sold its last three to Ion Media in December 2013, there were zero Black-owned and operated full-power TV stations in the US.
claims.evidence: TVNewsCheck (Dec 23, 2013): 18 in 2006 per Free Press, five by Dec 2012, zero after Roberts Broadcasting sold its three remaining full-power stations to ION Media Networks for ~$8M. LA Sentinel (2013) corroborates zero; notes Roberts' decline stemmed from Viacom shuttering UPN (its affiliate network).
claims.uncertainty: Low

claims.claim: Armstrong Williams' Howard Stirk Holdings became a significant Black station owner via Sinclair sidecar deals (WEYI Flint 2013, WWMB Myrtle Beach 2013, and 2014-15 Allbritton spinoffs in Alabama and Charleston); a Jan 2024 BET report said it operated seven stations.
claims.contradictory: Wikipedia's 2026 station table shows Howard Stirk currently owns four stations (WGWW, WSES, KHSV, WGWG) after selling WEYI (2026), WXBU (2026), and WWMB (2025); most stations are operated under LMAs/shared services with Sinclair — raising an ownership-vs-control question.
claims.evidence: Journal-isms (2013): Williams buying WEYI and WWMB; Wikipedia Armstrong Williams: full station tables with purchase/sale dates; BET (Jan 2024): operates seven stations nationwide.
claims.uncertainty: Current count and affiliation details shifting; Sinclair operational control via LMAs means 'Black-owned' ≠ independently operated.

claims.claim: DuJuan McCoy's Circle City Broadcasting won FCC approval (Feb/Mar 2026) to acquire the Indianapolis ABC affiliate from Scripps for $83M, giving the Black-owned group three stations — a rare expansion of Black broadcast ownership.
claims.evidence: Editor & Publisher/Broadband Breakfast (Mar 2, 2026): FCC Chairman Carr's FCC approved McCoy's Circle City Broadcasting acquisition of the local ABC affiliate from Scripps for $83M, giving CCB three stations total.
claims.uncertainty: Low — one of the freshest Black-ownership expansions on record.

claims.claim: WJYS (channel 62, Hammond IN/Chicago) is currently owned by Millennial Telecommunications, Inc.; its Black-owned status could NOT be verified in this pass — do not count it as Black-owned on assumption.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia WJYS: Owner listed as Millennial Telecommunications, Inc.; call-sign meaning 'Original owners Joseph and Yvonne Stroud' (historic, not current). No evidence found on the current owner's racial ownership.
claims.uncertainty: Current Black ownership unverified; historic Stroud ownership does not establish current ownership. Red-team: outdated ownership claims are common for this station.

entities.name: Blavity Inc.
entities.description: Venture-backed digital media company for Black millennials; owns Blavity, 21Ninety, Shadow and Act, Travel Noire, AfroTech, and Home & Texture, plus an ad network for publishers of color.

claims.claim: Blavity was founded in 2014 by CEO Morgan DeBaun with Aaron Samuels, Jonathan Jackson, and Jeff Nelson; the name combines 'black' and 'gravity'; it targets Black millennials.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'Blavity was founded by CEO Morgan DeBaun, Jonathan Jackson, Jeff Nelson, and Aaron Samuels in 2014'; Black Enterprise (2018) confirms founders and 2014 creation.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Blavity'; Black Enterprise, 'Blavity Founder Raises Over $6 Million in Funding' (2018)
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Blavity raised about $1M in a 500 Startups-led seed round (Sept 2016), ~$1.8M in follow-on seed funding (MACRO, New Media Ventures, Base Ventures, Cross Culture Ventures, Harlem Capital, Knight Enterprise Fund), and a $6.5M Series A led by GV in July 2018 (with Comcast Ventures, Plexo Capital, Baron Davis Enterprises), totaling ~$9.4M.
claims.contradictory: Techweek reported '~$2.9 million in a seed round... in 2016 and 2017,' an aggregation that differs from the itemized $1M + $1.8M figures; both derive from company statements.
claims.evidence: Black Enterprise (2018): '$6.5 million in new funding led by GV'; 'Prior to this Series A round, Blavity raised a little over $1.8 million'; Moguldom: 'An even earlier seed round led by 500 Startups raised $1 million, giving Blavity a total funding amount of $9.4 million.'
claims.uncertainty: Figures come from company announcements (primary but self-interested); secondary aggregations differ slightly. Treat totals as approximate.

claims.claim: In 2017 Blavity launched the Black women's lifestyle platform 21Ninety and acquired the Black entertainment site Shadow and Act and the Black travel site Travel Noire; in January 2023 it launched Home & Texture and restructured into Blavity Media Group and a DEI Solutions Group after doubling ad revenue in 2022.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (2017 launches/acquisitions; Jan 2023 Home & Texture); Adweek (2023): restructure into two divisions after 'two consecutive years of profitability' and doubled 2022 ad revenue, per CEO.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Blavity'; Adweek, 'Blavity, After Doubling Ad Revenue, Restructures and Launches New SaaS Product' (2023)
claims.uncertainty: Revenue figures are CEO-stated, not independently audited.

claims.claim: Blavity.com ranked #1 among Black-oriented websites in comScore averages (7.3M monthly uniques, up 120% over 2021), per Journal-isms' 2023 tally.
claims.evidence: Journal-isms: '1. Blavity.com, 7,297,000 unique monthly average visitors/viewers, up 120 percent over 2021.'
claims.source: Journal-isms, 'Blavity Rises to Most Popular Black Website'
claims.uncertainty: comScore panel methodology has been disputed by publishers in the past (e.g., The Root's publisher noted discrepancies in 2011).

claims.claim: CEO Morgan DeBaun said Blavity's Facebook page was once blocked after stories were flagged as 'too violent,' and that the company deliberately diversified revenue (conferences/AfroTech, Blavity Culture Network ad sales for publishers of color) because display advertising against news is unreliable.
claims.evidence: TechCrunch interview (July 2020): 'There was a time when our Facebook page was even blocked because [stories] have gotten flagged as being too violent... we do have this weird kind of balance... pushing back against our clients, our advertisers and even Facebook.'
claims.source: TechCrunch, 'Blavity has a big opportunity with Black millennials, despite struggling to fit the VC 'formula''
claims.uncertainty: Founder interview — primary but self-interested; a direct, named account of platform-moderation risk.

claims.claim: Blavity was founded in 2014 by Morgan DeBaun and co-founders as a digital media company for Black millennials; it raised $6.5 million in venture funding in 2018 led by GV (Google Ventures) with Comcast Ventures.
claims.evidence: Washington University alumni profile: DeBaun 'founded Blavity Inc. in 2014... raised $6.5 million in venture capital funding in 2018, led by GV (formerly Google Ventures), with participation from Comcast Ventures.'
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: Blavity grew by acquisition and diversification: it bought Shadow and Act and Travel Noire, operates the AfroTech conference (first held 2016), and its portfolio claims 100M+ monthly reach.
claims.evidence: HotPaths: Blavity 'acquired Shadow and Act... acquired Travel Noire... launched the AfroTech conference in 2016... its portfolio reaches over 100 million people per month.' Wikipedia: AfroTech 'first held in 2016.'
claims.uncertainty: The 100M reach figure is company-reported via a single secondary source.

claims.claim: In 2024-2025 Blavity Inc. was involved in a reported $12 million acquisition attempt by a BET-related investor group — a contested consolidation episode whose outcome was unclear as of research.
claims.evidence: Black Enterprise (Dec 2024): 'Blavity Founder Reportedly Rejects $12M Acquisition Attempt' by an investor group tied to BET Media Group.
claims.uncertainty: Single-source reporting on a disputed, unconsummated deal; treat as unresolved.

entities.name: BOMESI (Black Owned Media Equity and Sustainability Institute)
entities.description: The Black-owned-media equity institute (2020): documents the <2% ad-spend inequity and the revenue-diversification survival playbook for Black publishers.

claims.claim: BOMESI (Black Owned Media Equity and Sustainability Institute) launched around Juneteenth 2020 as a network of 300+ Black-owned publishers (plus 2,500 diverse-owned publishers), reaching a claimed 90 million households monthly.
claims.evidence: Adweek (Sept 2020): BOMESI is 'a network of 300-plus Black-owned publishers' launched 'around Juneteenth' 2020; 'Between them and 2,500 diverse-owned publishers, [BOMESI] reaches 90 million households every month.'
claims.uncertainty: Reach figure is network-reported; treat as company claim.

claims.claim: Black-owned media receive under 2% of total US advertising spend even though Black Americans are roughly 15% of the population, per Nielsen data cited by Adweek — the structural ad inequity BOMESI was built to address.
claims.evidence: Adweek: 'According to Nielsen, Black-owned media get less than 2% of total U.S. advertising spend, despite Black Americans comprising around 15% of the U.S. population.'
claims.uncertainty: Adweek's Nielsen attribution; the underlying Nielsen study was not independently reviewed here.

claims.claim: Black publishers responded to ad-commitment failures by diversifying revenue into subscriptions, memberships, events, branded content, and licensing.
claims.evidence: Adweek (2024): Black publishers built 'diversified revenue models... subscriptions, memberships, events, branded content and licensing' after advertiser commitments made in 2020 failed to materialize.
claims.uncertainty: Industry-trend reporting; not outlet-level financials.

entities.name: Bounce TV
entities.description: The first Black-targeted over-the-air multicast network (2011), now owned by Scripps; an example of the free-distribution-plus-advertising survival model — but no longer Black-owned.

claims.claim: Bounce TV was announced April 4, 2011 as the first 24/7 over-the-air broadcast network for African Americans, founded by Martin Luther King III, Ambassador Andrew Young, Andrew 'Bo' Young III, and filmmakers Rob Hardy and Will Packer, with execs Ryan Glover and Jonathan Katz; it launched September 26, 2011 at noon ET.
claims.evidence: TheWrap/The Futon Critic (Apr 4, 2011): Bounce announced as first-ever 24/7 broadcast net for African Americans; founders MLK III, Andrew Young, Bo Young III, Hardy, Packer; execs Ryan Glover, Jonathan Katz. TV Technology: launched Sept 26, 2011 at noon ET.
claims.source: TheWrap; The Futon Critic; TV Technology
claims.uncertainty: Low

claims.claim: Bounce was Black-owned at launch but was acquired by E.W. Scripps for $292 million; the purchase was announced August 1, 2017 and completed October 2, 2017. Bounce is now owned by Scripps Networks and is no longer Black-owned.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia Bounce TV: 'On August 1, 2017, E. W. Scripps announced the purchase of Bounce and Katz Broadcasting... for $292 million, acquiring the other 95% of the company... completed on October 2, 2017.' Parent now listed as Scripps Networks, LLC.
claims.uncertainty: Low — red-team: do not repeat Bounce as currently Black-owned. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

entities.name: FCC Minority Tax Certificate Program
entities.description: 1978-1995 FCC policy letting sellers of broadcast stations to minorities defer capital gains taxes; credited with the main wave of minority ownership growth; repealed 1995.

claims.claim: The FCC established the Minority Tax Certificate Program in 1978, providing a tax incentive to sellers of majority interests in broadcast stations to minorities; minority-owned stations grew from about 40 to 323 during the program.
claims.evidence: Radio-Online quoting NABOB's Jim Winston: 'from 1978 to 1995, the tax certificate boosted minority ownership significantly, raising the number of minority-owned stations from 40 to 323'; Congressional Record: minority ownership of all broadcast properties rose from 0.5% to 2.9% over the period.
claims.uncertainty: The 40-to-323 figure is a frequently cited aggregate; primary FCC data not re-verified here.

claims.claim: Congress repealed the program in 1995, after which minority broadcast station ownership declined sharply (Black Enterprise reports a 40% drop in minority-owned broadcast facilities and a 70% drop in African American ownership).
claims.evidence: 1978 Broadcast Policy Statement Wikipedia: repealed by Congress in 1995; Black Enterprise: 'the number of minority-owned broadcast facilities decreased by 40%. African American ownership decreased by 70%.'
claims.uncertainty: The 40%/70% figures come from advocacy reporting tied to repeal campaigns; exact denominators and time windows are not documented in the excerpts.

entities.name: Federal government advertising equity debate
entities.description: Ongoing dispute over whether federal advertising dollars reach Black-owned media; GAO data shows a tiny share going to Black-owned businesses, and NNPA demands reform.

claims.claim: A GAO study found the federal government spent more than $5 billion on advertising over five years (FY2014-2023), with Black-owned businesses receiving $51 million, or 1.02%; Black-owned businesses received $256 million (21%) of the $1.2 billion obligated to minority-owned businesses.
claims.contradictory: Different NNPA materials cite different totals ($5B over five years vs $14.9B), suggesting mixed timeframes; GAO's own definitions needed to reconcile.
claims.evidence: NNPA.org reporting GAO's figures and a clarifying email from GAO's Jessica Lucas-Judy.
claims.uncertainty: GAO figures reported secondhand by an advocacy outlet; the $5B figure and the $14.9B annual total cited elsewhere appear to cover different scopes/periods.

claims.claim: NNPA asserts Black-owned media received no more than $10 million of $14.9 billion in total federal ad spending, and notes only 14% of that $14.9B went to small disadvantaged businesses.
claims.evidence: NNPA.org statement; NNPA Chair quoted in journal-isms.com.
claims.uncertainty: Advocacy claim by an interested party; the $14.9B figure's scope/period is unclear and appears to differ from the GAO $5B/5-year figure.

claims.claim: In 2023 Rep. Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the Federal Government Advertising Equity Accountability Act, requiring federal agencies to detail ad spending with small, disadvantaged, women- and minority-owned businesses in annual budget justifications.
claims.evidence: NNPA.org reporting on the bill.
claims.uncertainty: Low for introduction; enactment status not verified in this research.

entities.name: Frankie Crocker
entities.description: Legendary Black radio DJ and programmer who coined the term 'urban contemporary' and programmed WBLS in the 1970s-80s.

claims.claim: Crocker coined the term 'urban contemporary' in the early to mid-1970s as a synonym for Black music.
claims.evidence: Urban contemporary Wikipedia: 'The term was coined by New York radio DJ Frankie Crocker in the early to mid-1970s as a synonym for Black music.'
claims.uncertainty: Low; widely attributed. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

claims.claim: As program director at Inner City's WBLS, Crocker built the 'Total Black Experience in Sound' and a dominant mid-1970s to early-1980s run that set the urban contemporary template.
claims.evidence: Inner City Wikipedia: WBLS 'pioneered the urban contemporary format under program director Frankie Crocker' with the 'Total Black Experience in Sound' slogan.
claims.uncertainty: Contributions of other programmers (Barry Mayo et al.) are also credited in oral histories. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

claims.evidence: Wikipedia, 'The Root (magazine)' history section.
claims.uncertainty: Low. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

claims.source: AV Club, 'The Root, G/O Media's last remaining website, finds a new home'; Journal-isms (2025)
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.uncertainty: Low; wind-down consistently reported across outlets.

entities.name: Getty Research Institute
entities.description: The Getty Trust's research institute; joint owner of the JPC Archive and funder/leader of its multi-year digitization.

claims.claim: The Getty Research Institute (a program of the J. Paul Getty Trust) is joint owner of the Johnson Publishing Company Archive and leads its processing and digitization, backed by a $30 million Getty Trust commitment.
claims.evidence: Hyperallergic: ownership 'formally transferred jointly to the Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture (NMAAHC) and the Getty Research Institute. Sold for $30 million in 2019... The Getty Trust is further committing $30 million to the organization and digitization of the archive.'
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: The archive's photo files were built beginning in 1949 by librarian Doris Saunders and expanded under photo editor Basil Phillips, preserving published and unpublished images from the mid-1940s through the early 2000s.
claims.evidence: Getty/NMAAHC panel 'Backstage: An Unfurling of the Johnson Publishing Company' (May 15, 2025): 'Visionary librarian Doris Saunders established the Johnson Publishing Company's (JPC) meticulously organized and unparalleled photo files beginning in 1949... Under her successor, photo editor Basil Phillips, the collection significantly grew... spanning from the mid-1940s through the early 2000s.'
claims.uncertainty: Event-description text, not a catalog record; but it reflects the holding institutions' own framing.

entities.name: Google Search / AI Overviews
entities.description: Google Search and its AI Overviews: the dominant discovery layer for Black publishers, where algorithm updates and zero-click answers threaten referral traffic.

claims.claim: Google's September 2023 Helpful Content Update sharply reduced search visibility for many independent publishers; one detailed publisher account reported ~40% traffic loss and a 34% ad-revenue drop, with peers reporting up to 90% losses.
claims.evidence: ppc.land (Jan 2025): 'The decline began following Google's 'Helpful Content Update' in September 2023... advertising revenue dropped 34% year-over-year in 2024... Some of her colleagues have reported losses of up to 90% in both traffic and revenue.'
claims.source: ppc.land, 'Travel blogger loses 40% traffic after Google changes spark industry crisis'
claims.uncertainty: The update's existence is verified; severity figures come from self-reported publisher accounts, not independent measurement.

claims.claim: From 2024, Google's AI Overviews began summarizing publisher journalism atop search results; BET (2025) warned that Black-owned sites like The Grio, Blavity, Okayplayer, and AfroTech — which 'depend on every single visitor to stay alive' — lack the cushion of conglomerates like Penske (which is suing Google over AI Overviews).
claims.evidence: BET: 'Black-owned sites like The Grio, Blavity, Okayplayer, AfroTech, and countless local newsrooms don't have that cushion. A drop in traffic could mean layoffs, reduced coverage, or shutting down entirely.'
claims.source: BET, 'When Google AI Summarizes, Black Websites Pay the Price'
claims.uncertainty: Analysis/opinion piece; names outlets as at-risk but does not attribute specific traffic losses to AI Overviews at any one outlet.

claims.claim: comScore's 2023 averages showed broad declines across Black-oriented sites: TheRoot.com -36%, MadameNoire -22%, AtlantaBlackStar -16.1%, NewsOne -20%, EURweb -63%, Andscape -61% — while Blavity.com (+120%) and Bossip (+50%) grew.
claims.evidence: Journal-isms (2023) full comScore table for Black-oriented websites.
claims.source: Journal-isms, 'Blavity Rises to Most Popular Black Website'
claims.uncertainty: comScore panel methodology disputed by some publishers; declines are correlational with (not proven caused by) search/social changes.

entities.name: Graham Holdings (Washington Post Company)

claims.evidence: Journal-isms 2015: 'Pinkie Mayfield, a spokeswoman for Graham Holdings, formerly the Washington Post Co., told Journal-isms that Univision approached Graham Holdings.'
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Group Black
entities.description: Black media collective and ad-sales intermediary founded in 2021 to redirect brand dollars to Black-owned publishers; stumbled amid missed targets, executive departures, and lawsuits.

claims.claim: Group Black was founded in June 2021 by Richelieu Dennis, Bonin Bough, and Travis Montaque as a media collective/accelerator to channel brand ad spending to 150+ Black-owned publishers; GroupM committed an initial $75M toward a stated goal of deploying $500M.
claims.evidence: Adweek (2021): founders 'announced an initial investment of $75 million from the agency GroupM... part of Group Black's broader effort to deploy at least $500 million in Black-owned media'; AfroTech: 'co-founded in June 2021 by Richelieu Dennis, Bonin Bough, and Travis Montaque.'
claims.source: Adweek, 'GroupM Invests $75 Million in Black-Owned Media'; AfroTech
claims.uncertainty: Low for founding and GroupM commitment; the $500M was a stated goal, not raised capital.

claims.claim: By 2024–2025 the $500M goal had fallen short; Montaque and Dennis departed; Essence Communications sued Group Black (May 2025) alleging $7M in unpaid bills (after a dismissed Oct 2024 suit alleging $20M), and Group Black countersued claiming a January 2024 debt-to-equity agreement.
claims.contradictory: Group Black admits the $7M debt but claims Dennis agreed to convert it to equity and then reversed course — the obligation itself is disputed.
claims.evidence: Adweek (2025): 'By 2024, the company had grown quiet... grumblings of late payments... That summer, Montaque... quietly left... Dennis... left the collective shortly after'; AfroTech (2025) on the dual lawsuits.
claims.source: Adweek, 'Inside the Dual Lawsuits Threatening to Unravel Group Black'; AfroTech
claims.uncertainty: Litigation facts verified via reporting; underlying financial claims are contested allegations.

claims.claim: In 2023 Group Black placed a reported $400M bid to acquire Vice Media (per the Wall Street Journal, relayed by AfroTech).
claims.evidence: AfroTech: 'According to The Wall Street Journal, Group Black... has reportedly placed a $400 million bid to acquire Vice Media.'
claims.source: AfroTech, 'Group Black... Places $400M Bid To Acquire Vice Media'
claims.uncertainty: Relayed second-hand from the WSJ; bid outcome not established in this research pass.

claims.evidence: History of radio disc jockeys Wikipedia: 'In 1939, Hal Jackson was the first African American radio sportscaster at WOOK-AM in Washington, DC, and later hosted The House That Jack Built.'

claims.uncertainty: None material. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

claims.evidence: New Pittsburgh Courier Wikipedia, quoting Sengstacke's appointment statement and the 1976 award.

claims.evidence: Publisher Karen Carter Richards' own account (Comcast/365 Houston interview) and Congressional Record agree on the 1960 founding and three-generation succession.

claims.claim: Described as the largest independently owned and operated African-American newspaper in the Southwest/South, reaching over three-fourths of Houston's African-American population, with a staff of about 15; the US House honored its 50th anniversary (H.Res. 160, 2011).

claims.uncertainty: Low.
