claims.evidence: Radio Facts industry commentary.
claims.uncertainty: Medium; reported by a single trade-commentary outlet.

entities.name: Inner City Broadcasting Corporation
entities.description: Pioneering Black-owned broadcast company (Percy Sutton, Clarence Jones and 50+ Black shareholders); acquired WLIB in 1972 and pioneered the urban contemporary format with WBLS. Historical anchor of Black-owned radio.

claims.claim: Inner City was founded in 1970 by Percy Sutton and others, with WLIB (later WBLS-FM) as its first acquisitions; WBLS pioneered the urban contemporary format under program director Frankie Crocker.
claims.evidence: Inner City Wikipedia: first acquisition WLIB AM 1972, WLIB-FM (renamed WBLS) two years later; 'WBLS would experience a period of tremendous success from the mid-1970s to the early 1980s as it pioneered the urban contemporary format under program director Frankie Crocker.' Black Enterprise (2003): 'The originator of the urban contemporary radio format 30 years ago, Inner City Broadcasting Corp.'
claims.uncertainty: The term 'urban contemporary' is also credited to Frankie Crocker's coining; format pioneers overlap with Barry Mayo and others.

claims.claim: ICBC entered Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2011 ($254 million debt); on October 19, 2012 YMF Media LLC (Ron Burkle + Magic Johnson) acquired majority control of its 15 stations for $180 million, then broke up the group in 2013-2014 sales.
claims.evidence: Inner City Wikipedia: creditors petitioned Aug 22, 2011; 'majority control ... taken over by YMF Media LLC, controlled jointly by investor Ronald Burkle and former NBA player Earvin "Magic" Johnson'; 'YMF Media eventually purchased 15 Inner City stations for $180 million on October 19, 2012; the firm then broke up the group in a series of subsequent sales during 2013-2014.'
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Inner City Broadcasting was founded in 1970 by prominent Black New Yorkers led by Percy Sutton and Clarence Jones; it acquired WLIB in 1972 and later WBLS, pioneering the urban contemporary format under Frankie Crocker.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia summary of the company's history.
claims.uncertainty: Medium; single secondary encyclopedic source.

entities.name: Jack Gibson ('Jack the Rapper')
entities.description: WERD's star DJ from 1949, originator of the fast-talking rhyming patter that influenced hip-hop; later founded the Black radio convention/trade paper 'Jack the Rapper.'

claims.claim: Gibson was hired at WERD soon after Blayton's purchase and by 1951 was the most popular DJ in Atlanta; his slang-and-rhyme announcing style influenced later generations of DJs.
claims.evidence: WAEC Wikipedia: '"Jockey" Jack Gibson was hired soon after, and by 1951 was the most popular DJ in Atlanta'; Smithsonian: his announcing style 'influenced subsequent generations of DJs'; Dan Charnas, The Big Payback, documents the connection to later hip-hop patter.
claims.uncertainty: 'Most popular DJ in Atlanta' is a contemporary trade-press judgment; influence on hip-hop is widely argued but interpretive.

claims.claim: Gibson is regarded as 'the father of the Black appeal radio format' and founded the annual 'Jack the Rapper' Family Affair convention (1977-2000), a Black music industry trade convention.
claims.evidence: Joseph Deighton Gibson Jr. Wikipedia: 'regarded as the father of the Black appeal radio format'; Lexology trademark case: founded and hosted until his death in 2000 the annual convention.
claims.uncertainty: 'Father of Black appeal' is an honorific also given to others; the convention is documented.

entities.name: Jack L. Cooper
entities.description: Vaudeville performer turned radio pioneer, widely credited as the first African American to make a career in radio broadcasting.

claims.claim: Cooper created and hosted 'The All-Negro Hour,' which premiered November 3, 1929 on Chicago's WSBC, the first radio program to feature an exclusively African American cast of performers.
claims.contradictory: Ellett's research documents two Black series prior to 1929 that lacked lecture/informative framing.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia 'The All-Negro Hour' cites the program's Nov 3, 1929 premiere on WSBC as the first all-Black-cast radio program; Ryan Ellett's Old Time Radio researchers note two earlier Black-cast series in 1927-1928, complicating any absolute 'first' claim.
claims.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_All-Negro_Hour; Ryan Ellett, 'Uncovering Black Radio's Roots: 1927-1929' (OTRR); teachrock.org 'Pioneers of Early Black Radio'
claims.uncertainty: Ellett argues two earlier Black-cast series aired in 1927-1928, so 'first' depends on definition (first with serial sketches vs first ever).

claims.claim: Cooper later became Chicago's first Black sportscaster, newscaster, and radio executive, and eventually owned a radio station.
claims.evidence: African American Registry biography states Cooper became 'the city's first black sportscaster, newscaster, and radio executive' and 'went on to own his radio station.'
claims.uncertainty: The station he owned is not named in the source.

entities.name: Jesse B. Blayton Sr.
entities.description: Atlanta accountant, bank president, and Atlanta University professor who bought WERD in 1949, making it the first radio station both owned and programmed by African Americans.

claims.claim: Blayton purchased WERD in 1949 for $50,000, making it the first radio station owned and operated by African Americans.
claims.evidence: WAEC (AM) Wikipedia: Blayton purchased WERD in 1949 for $50,000; Atlanta Journal-Constitution confirms the 1949 $50,000 purchase; Donna Halper (2008): 'Black entrepreneurs had tried since 1930 to buy a radio station, but they remained unsuccessful till 1949.'
claims.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WAEC_(AM); AJC; gregorturk.com WERD history by Donna L. Halper
claims.uncertainty: Low; consistently reported across independent sources.

claims.claim: WERD's format targeted Black listeners with R&B, jazz, gospel, public-service and educational programming; its Auburn Avenue (Masonic building) studios shared a building with the SCLC/Dr. King.
claims.contradictory: Community Sentinel article: original location was Broad Street, not Auburn Avenue as commonly told.
claims.evidence: Jesse B. Blayton Wikipedia: programming oriented toward African-Americans, pioneering R&B format; SCLC shared the building; Marsha Washington George notes the station was originally on Broad Street (white country music station) before relocation to the Prince Hall Masonic Grand Lodge.
claims.uncertainty: The MLK-mic-out-the-window story is widely repeated but its literal details are disputed; the Auburn vs Broad Street origin is a documented correction.

claims.claim: Blayton sold WERD in 1968; the frequency (now 860 WAEC) went dark in 2024 after Beasley Media sold the tower site.
claims.evidence: Blayton Wikipedia: sold WERD in 1968; AJC 2024: 860 WAEC went dark after 76 years when Beasley Media sold the 17.2-acre tower site to Toll Brothers.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

entities.name: Jet
entities.description: Pocket-size Black newsweekly founded 1951 by John H. Johnson; famous for publishing the Emmett Till open-casket photos (1955); ended print in June 2014, continuing digitally.

claims.claim: Founded November 1, 1951 by John H. Johnson as "The Weekly Negro News Magazine" - a digest-size weekly for African-American news, culture and "Beauty of the Week."
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (Nov 1, 1951, founder) and Johnson Publishing Company history agree.
claims.uncertainty: Low. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

claims.claim: In 1955 Jet published photographs of Emmett Till's open casket at the request of his mother Mamie Till Bradley, a landmark act of civil-rights photojournalism that brought the lynching's brutality to national attention.
claims.evidence: NPR (Karen Grigsby Bates) and the Oklahoma Eagle recount Johnson's decision and its impact.
claims.source: NPR via KSUT, 2014-05-07; The Oklahoma Eagle, 2019-04-19
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Jet reduced frequency from weekly to biweekly in 2011, then ended regular print publication in June 2014 (720,000 print circulation at the time), converting to a digital magazine app in July 2014 with an annual special print edition.
claims.evidence: AP (via phys.org, May 7, 2014): print ends end of June, digital app; Wikipedia: final print issue June 2014; JPC Wikipedia: weekly to biweekly 2011, digital-only July 2014.
claims.source: Associated Press via phys.org, 2014-05-07; Wikipedia (Jet; Johnson Publishing Company); NPR Illinois, 2014-05-08
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Jet (with Ebony) was sold to Clear View Group in 2016; Jet had been the No. 3 magazine in the African-American market behind Ebony and Essence.
claims.evidence: CJR and Oklahoma Eagle on the 2016 sale; Urban Daily on market rank.
claims.source: CJR; The Oklahoma Eagle, 2019-04-19; The Urban Daily, 2014-05-07
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Jet was founded by JPC in 1951 as a weekly digest of Black news; its September 1955 issue published Mamie Till's open-coffin photograph of Emmett Till, catalyzing the civil rights movement.
claims.evidence: Okeagle.com: 'Jet, founded in 1951 as a weekly news digest... published the open-casket photograph of Emmett Till in September 1955, a decision that galvanized the Civil Rights Movement.' Ebony.com: 'In 1951, JET magazine—a weekly digest of Black news—came along.'
claims.uncertainty: None material; widely corroborated.

claims.claim: Jet ceased print publication in 2014, becoming digital-only, as print advertising collapsed and internet competition intensified.
claims.evidence: Okeagle: 'Jet ceased print publication in 2014, transitioning to a digital-only format.' CJR: 'Print revenue dropped, and advertising dollars shrunk.'
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: Jet was sold with Ebony to Clear View Group in 2016 and then to Bridgeman Sports and Media for $14 million in December 2020.
claims.evidence: CJR and Black Enterprise coverage of the 2016 Clear View sale and the 2020 Bridgeman purchase ('bought Ebony Magazine and Jet Magazine out of bankruptcy for $14 million in December 2020').
claims.uncertainty: None material.

entities.name: John H. Sengstacke
entities.description: Chicago Defender publisher who organized the 1940 founding of the NNPA and built a four-paper national Black newspaper chain (Michigan Chronicle, Tri-State Defender, New Pittsburgh Courier); served on Truman's military-integration commission.

claims.claim: Sengstacke organized the 1940 meeting of Black publishers that founded the NNPA (originally the National Negro Publishers Association).
claims.evidence: Multiple sources (African American Registry, NNPA coverage, Wikipedia mirrors).
claims.source: African American Registry; Savannah Tribune via NNPA
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: He built a national chain of Black newspapers: founded the Michigan Chronicle (1936), owned the Tri-State Defender (Memphis), and bought and relaunched the Pittsburgh Courier as the New Pittsburgh Courier (1965-67).
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (Michigan Chronicle; New Pittsburgh Courier); Savannah Tribune (chain list).
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: In 1947 he co-founded Americans for Democratic Action; President Truman named him to the 1948 commission to integrate the armed forces; in 1956 he converted the Chicago Defender from weekly to daily.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (John Sengstacke).
claims.uncertainty: Low. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

claims.claim: He died in 1997; his papers were held in a family trust until their 2003 sale to Real Times for nearly $12 million.
claims.evidence: New Pittsburgh Courier Wikipedia.
claims.uncertainty: Low. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

entities.name: Johnson Publishing Company
entities.description: John H. Johnson's Chicago-based publishing empire (Ebony, Jet, Negro Digest); bankruptcy in 2019 ended corporate Black-press scale in Chicago and scattered its archive to a foundation rescue.

claims.claim: John H. Johnson founded the Johnson Publishing Company in 1942, building it from a $500 loan into the publisher of Ebony (1945) and Jet (1951).
claims.evidence: Ebony.com history: 'Johnson Publishing Company (JPC) — the media empire founded by John H. Johnson in 1942... In 1945, Johnson launched EBONY magazine... In 1951, JET magazine... came along.' Columbia Journalism Review corroborates the $500-loan origin story.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: After Johnson's death in 2005 the company declined; JPC sold its magazines to Clear View Group in 2016 and filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in April 2019, after which its photo archive was auctioned for $30 million.
claims.evidence: Okeagle.com bankruptcy summary: 'In 2016, JPC sold its flagship brands, Ebony and Jet, to Clear View Group LLC... In April 2019, JPC filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy, liquidating its assets.' CJR notes the magazine sale and bankruptcy sequence.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: In 2010 JPC sold its landmark Michigan Avenue headquarters tower to Columbia College Chicago; the building sale was one of the company's last major assets before bankruptcy.
claims.evidence: NPR/WAMC (2010): 'The Johnson Publishing Company has sold its landmark Michigan Avenue building to Columbia College.'
claims.uncertainty: None material.

entities.name: Johnson Publishing Company Archive
entities.description: The photographic and audiovisual archive of Johnson Publishing Company (Ebony, Jet, Negro Digest): 3-4 million images plus TV/radio recordings, rescued from bankruptcy and now jointly owned by the Smithsonian NMAAHC and the Getty Research Institute.

claims.claim: In July 2019 a consortium of the Ford Foundation, the J. Paul Getty Trust, the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation, and the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation acquired the Johnson Publishing Company archive for $30 million at the company's bankruptcy auction.
claims.contradictory: The Art Newspaper (2022) describes the consortium as the four foundations plus the Smithsonian Institution as purchaser; Pulitzer.org (2019) names four foundations. The discrepancy is whether the Smithsonian was a co-purchaser or a planned recipient.
claims.evidence: Pulitzer.org announcement, July 25, 2019: 'A consortium of four foundations has acquired the archive of Johnson Publishing Company, publisher of Ebony and Jet magazines for $30 million... The Ford Foundation, The J. Paul Getty Trust, the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation and the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation jointly announced the acquisition.'
claims.uncertainty: Low on price and buyers; minor discrepancy on Smithsonian's role in the purchase noted above.

claims.claim: On July 28, 2022, ownership of the JPC archive was formally transferred jointly to the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture (NMAAHC) and the Getty Research Institute; the archive is physically housed at the NMAAHC in Washington, DC.
claims.evidence: The Art Newspaper, Aug 1, 2022: 'its vast and partially unexplored archive has landed in the joint ownership of the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture (NMAAHC)... and California's Getty Research Institute... the archive will be physically housed at the NMAAHC in Washington, DC.' Corroborated by Hyperallergic and EURweb.
claims.uncertainty: None material; transfer date confirmed by multiple outlets.

claims.claim: The archive comprises more than 3 million photo negatives and slides, 983,000 photographs, 166,000 contact sheets, and 9,000 audio and visual recordings, including Ebony/Jet Showcase TV recordings and segments from radio stations Johnson owned.
claims.contradictory: Other reputable reports round the total to 'more than four million prints and negatives' (Hyperallergic; Pulitzer). The figures are consistent in magnitude but differ in breakdown.
claims.evidence: The Art Newspaper: 'more than 3 million photo negatives and slides, 983,000 photographs, 166,000 contact sheets and 9,000 audio and visual recordings.' Columbia Journalism Review adds the A/V includes 'audio and video recordings of Johnson's television productions—such as the Ebony Jet Showcase and the annual Black Achievement Awards—plus segments from radio stations that Johnson owned.'
claims.uncertainty: Low; figures come from the consortium/institutions. A/V specifics (radio segments) per CJR reporting.

claims.claim: The Getty Trust committed $30 million to the organization and digitization of the archive; portions are being made accessible to the public during the ongoing multi-year digitization process.
claims.evidence: Hyperallergic: 'The Getty Trust is further committing $30 million to the organization and digitization of the archive, which will allow researchers easier access to its holdings.' EURweb: 'With work already underway, portions of the archive will be accessible to the public during the ongoing intensive digitization process.'
claims.uncertainty: Completion timeline uncertain: CJR (2023) reported the team was in 'year two of a seven-year undertaking'; a 2025 panel described a commitment to public availability by 2029. Treat end-date as provisional.

entities.name: Karen Carter Richards
entities.description: Third-generation publisher/CEO of the Houston Forward Times (since 2010); elected NNPA national chair in 2019; 2018 NNPA Publisher of the Year.

claims.claim: Richards took over the Houston Forward Times in 2010 after her mother Lenora "Doll" Carter's death, continuing the family line begun by her father Julius P. Carter in 1960; her daughters Chelsea (general manager) and Nykayla (social media editor) also work at the paper.
claims.evidence: Richards' own interviews (Comcast/365 Houston; Post News Group).
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: She was elected NNPA national chair in June 2019, succeeding Dorothy Leavell, and had won the 2018 NNPA Publisher of the Year award.
claims.evidence: Los Angeles Sentinel and Post News Group reporting.
claims.source: Los Angeles Sentinel, 2019-06-28; Post News Group
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: KCOH Houston
entities.description: Historic Black-owned Houston station (first Black-owned station in Texas, 1953); the 1430 signal was sold to a Catholic broadcaster in 2013.

claims.claim: In 1953 Robert C. Meeker bought KCOH and made it the first Black-owned radio station in Texas (reportedly the third in the nation) with all-Negro programming.
claims.evidence: Black Enterprise (2012): 'in 1953, Robert C. Meeker bought the radio station, defining it as the first black owned radio station in Texas, third in the nation and the second oldest AM station in Houston to keep its original call letters.'
claims.uncertainty: 'Third in the nation' claim is an institutional memory figure; not independently verified.

claims.claim: KCOH sold its 1430 signal in November 2012 to the La Promesa Foundation (Guadalupe Radio Network) for $2,141,000; after 59 years it ended as a Black-owned station.
claims.evidence: RadioInsight (2013): 'KCOH sold its 1430 signal in November to the La Promesa Foundation for $2,141,000'; Black Enterprise: sold for $2.1 million, 'ends a 59-year history of serving Houston's Black community.' The format later relaunched on 1230 AM under different ownership.
claims.uncertainty: Low on the sale; the post-2019 1230 KCOH 'The Source' revival is owned by Pueblo de Galilea (Radio Aleluya), not the original Black owners.

entities.name: Lauren Williams
entities.description: Former Vox editor-in-chief; co-founder and CEO of the nonprofit newsroom Capital B.

claims.claim: Lauren Williams, formerly SVP and editor-in-chief of Vox, left to co-found the nonprofit news organization Capital B with Akoto Ofori-Atta (then managing editor of The Trace); they conceived it in June 2020 after the George Floyd protests and launched January 31, 2022.
claims.evidence: NPR (Feb 2022): Williams 'had been editor-in-chief of Vox, and Ofori-Atta, who had been the managing editor at The Trace'; 'We conceived of Capital B in June of 2020'; Digiday: 'officially launched on Jan. 31.'
claims.source: NPR, 'Capital B is a new media outlet focused on a Black audience'; Digiday Podcast
claims.uncertainty: Low; launch narrative from founders (primary, self-interested).

claims.claim: Williams previously worked at The Root (with Ofori-Atta, whom she met there in 2010) and at Mother Jones; she chose the nonprofit model to avoid advertiser/subscriber pressure.
claims.evidence: E&P: 'Williams was previously senior vice president and editor-in-chief of Vox and an editor at Mother Jones and The Root... 'Akoto and I met in 2010 while working at The Root.''; Digiday on the nonprofit rationale.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Library of Congress (Chronicling America / microfilm program)
entities.description: The Library of Congress's free digitized newspaper program (Chronicling America) and its 1947 microfilming project: the backbone of public access to historic Black newspapers.

claims.claim: In 1947 the Library of Congress and the American Council of Learned Societies microfilmed more than 150 African American newspapers (12 reels) as one of the largest and earliest microfilming projects in US history; for some titles, only a single issue is extant.
claims.evidence: LOC Civil War Black Washington research guide: 'In 1947 the Library of Congress and the American Council of Learned Societies... carried out one of the largest and earliest microfilming projects in US history by microfilming over 150 African American newspapers... The project comprised 12 reels of microfilm. For some titles, only a single issue is extant.'
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: By February 2022 the LOC had digitized 568 issues of three Frederick Douglass titles (North Star 137 issues, Frederick Douglass' Paper 220, New National Era 211) and made them freely available in Chronicling America.
claims.evidence: InfoDocket: 'Frederick Douglass Newspapers, 1847-1874: Now Online Via Chronicling America... 568 issues have been digitized including: The North Star: 137 issues; Frederick Douglass' Paper: 220 issues; New National Era: 211 issues.'
claims.uncertainty: None material; corroborated by LOC.

claims.claim: In February 2022 the LOC added another 1,224 pages from 103 African American newspaper titles to Chronicling America, on top of 110+ African American titles already digitized by state participants in the National Digital Newspaper Program.
claims.evidence: InfoDocket: 'In February 2022, the Library of Congress added another 1,224 pages from 103 African American newspaper titles to its digitized collections... added to 110-plus other African American newspapers that have been digitized by the institutions and organizations that have participated in the National Digital Newspaper Program.'
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: Chronicling America access is free; the LOC's subscription-database guide separately lists the commercial Readex African American Newspapers collection (350+ publications) as a paywalled institutional resource.
claims.evidence: LOC guide: 'The African American Newspapers collection... available online for free via Chronicling America.' The same guide lists 'African American Newspapers, 1827-1998 (Readex)' under Subscription Databases: '350+ publications from 35 states, spanning from 1827 to 1998.'
claims.uncertainty: None.

entities.name: Los Angeles Sentinel
entities.description: Los Angeles weekly founded 1933; the largest paid-subscription Black-owned weekly on the West Coast; owned since 2004 by Danny Bakewell.

claims.claim: Founded in 1933 by Leon H. Washington Jr. (first issue May 17, 1933); it began as the Eastside Shopper serving the Central Avenue district before becoming the Sentinel.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia and the paper's own About page: founded 1933 by Col. Leon H. Washington; African American Registry: first issue May 17, 1933; BlackAmericaWeb: began as Eastside Shopper.
claims.source: Wikipedia (Los Angeles Sentinel); lasentinel.net/about; African American Registry; BlackAmericaWeb, 2018
claims.uncertainty: Low for founding year; specific first-issue date from single registry source.

claims.claim: After Washington's death, his wife Ruth Washington took over as publisher and editor in 1974 and led the paper until her death in 1990.
claims.evidence: BlackAmericaWeb and the paper's own About page agree on Ruth Washington's 1974-1990 tenure.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Attorney Kenneth R. Thomas and Jennifer Thomas purchased the Sentinel in 1983 (Thomas president/CEO 1990-1997, Jennifer 1997-2004); on March 17, 2004 it was purchased by real estate developer and community activist Danny Bakewell, who became executive publisher, chairman and CEO.
claims.evidence: The paper's own About page details the Thomas era and the March 2004 Bakewell purchase.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: The Sentinel claims ~125,000 readers (2004), ABC-audited paid circulation, the largest paid Black-owned newspaper in the West; distribution contracted to the Los Angeles Times with USPS delivery outside metro LA.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia ("boasted of reaching 125,000 readers as of 2004") and the paper's own materials claim ABC-audited paid status; figures are self-reported.
claims.uncertainty: Medium: readership figures are self-reported and dated.

entities.name: Loud Speakers Network
entities.description: Podcast network known for Black-culture shows like The Read and The Friend Zone; co-founded by Chris Morrow and the late Reggie Ossé — marketed toward Black audiences but not Black-founded.

claims.claim: Loud Speakers Network was co-founded by Chris Morrow and Reggie Ossé and is home to shows including The Read, The Friend Zone, Brilliant Idiots, and the Combat Jack Show.
claims.evidence: RAIN News interview with CEO Chris Morrow ('When Reggie and I started LSN...'); Everand/Dreams in Drive (2018): Morrow is 'CEO and co-founder of Loud Speakers Network- home of... The Read, The Friendzone... and the infamous The Combat Jack Show.'
claims.source: RAIN News, 'The Loud Speakers Network Gets Loud – An Interview with CEO Chris Morrow'; Everand, Dreams in Drive Podcast
claims.uncertainty: Exact founding year not established in this research pass.

claims.claim: CEO Chris Morrow describes himself as 'a middle aged white guy' and says the network set out to be a platform for African-American and POC voices — i.e., it is marketed as a Black podcast network but was not Black-founded or Black-owned.
claims.evidence: RAIN News: 'as a middle aged white guy, I don't think it's for me to say what's black and what isn't... When Reggie and I started LSN, the goal was to provide a platform for African-Americans and POC in podcasting.'
claims.source: RAIN News interview with Chris Morrow
claims.uncertainty: Ownership/audience positioning verified via the CEO's own words; a useful red-team case for verifying 'Black-owned' podcast claims.

entities.name: Media Rating Council (MRC)
entities.description: Independent industry body that accredits audience-measurement services; the arbiter of ratings currency legitimacy. Suspended Nielsen's TV accreditation in 2021 and restored it in 2023.

claims.claim: The MRC suspended accreditation of Nielsen's national TV ratings in September 2021 — its first such action — and restored national accreditation in April 2023 after audits showed compliance; it later accredited Nielsen's Big Data + Panel solution (January 2025).
claims.evidence: NewsLab, MarTech, Advanced Television, AdTechRadar.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Melvin Lindsey
entities.description: WHUR-FM intern-turned-host who originated the 'Quiet Storm' late-night format in 1976, which became the industry standard for urban adult radio nights.

claims.claim: In 1976 Lindsey brought 'The Quiet Storm' to Howard University's WHUR-FM late-night lineup, titled after Smokey Robinson's song; the love-song-heavy format was quickly replicated at urban stations nationwide.
claims.contradictory: Quiet storm Wikipedia notes WDAS-FM Philadelphia ran a similar format starting 1972 and adopted the 'Quiet Storm' name in 1976.
claims.evidence: Radio Hall of Fame: 'In 1976, he brought the "Quiet Storm" to the station's late-night lineup'; Quiet storm Wikipedia: within a few years 'virtually every station in the U.S. with a core black, urban listenership adopted a similar format for its graveyard slot.'
claims.uncertainty: WDAS-FM Philadelphia is noted as having a similar 1972 format ('The Extrasensory Connection,' renamed Quiet Storm in 1976), complicating sole-credit claims.

claims.claim: After nine years at WHUR, Lindsey took the format to WKYS-FM for five more years; he died in 1992 at 36.
claims.evidence: Melvin Lindsey Wikipedia; Radio Hall of Fame.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

entities.name: Meta platforms (Facebook/Instagram)
entities.description: Meta's Facebook (and Instagram) distribution infrastructure: the January 2018 feed-algorithm shift and 2024 News-tab deprecation that repeatedly stranded publishers built on its traffic.

claims.claim: In January 2018 Facebook shifted its News Feed to prioritize 'meaningful interactions' (friends/family), cutting publishers' organic reach; Chartbeat measured Facebook referral traffic down 15% in 2017 and another 6% from January 2018, with Facebook warning news's feed share would fall from ~5% to ~4% (implying ~20% reach cuts).
claims.evidence: Digiday (Feb 2018): 'Chartbeat data showed Facebook traffic to publishers declined 6 percent since the beginning of January'; Facebook: 'news publishers' reach on the platform may go down'; Adweek: the shift 'is hurting a number of digital publishers, particularly startups that have come to rely almost exclusively on organic traffic from Facebook.'
claims.source: Digiday, 'As promised, Facebook traffic to news publishers declines again'; Adweek, 'Here's How Facebook's Algorithm Shift Is Hurting Digital Publishers'
claims.uncertainty: Low for the shift and measured declines.

claims.claim: Platform-dependent publishers were the casualties: LittleThings shut down in February 2018 after Facebook traffic fell ~70% following the tweak; Cox Media shut down Rare after its traffic 'evaporated.'
claims.evidence: CJR: 'Another Facebook-focused publisher, Little Things, shut down in February after saying its Facebook traffic had fallen by about 70 percent following the latest algorithm tweak'; Rare 'shutting down after traffic evaporated.'
claims.source: CJR, 'Another news site that relied on Facebook shuts down'
claims.uncertainty: Neither outlet was Black-owned; included as the documented template of platform-dependence risk.

claims.claim: Named Black-outlet exposure: Blavity's Facebook page was once blocked over 'violent' content flags (DeBaun, TechCrunch 2020); Atlanta Black Star participates in a Facebook partnership program; Black Star News was among 400 outlets receiving a $5,000 Facebook COVID grant.
claims.evidence: TechCrunch (2020) DeBaun interview; Wikipedia 'Atlanta Black Star'; Wikipedia 'Black Star News': 'one of 400 news organizations to receive a $5,000 grant from Facebook to mitigate unexpected expenses due to COVID-19.'
claims.uncertainty: Low for the individual facts; no Black outlet publicly attributed a shutdown to Facebook changes in this research pass.

claims.claim: In February/March 2024 Meta deprecated the Facebook News tab in the US and Australia (after the UK, France, Germany in 2023), stopped entering new commercial news deals, and said news is under 3% of feed content.
claims.evidence: TechCrunch (Feb 29, 2024): Meta 'will sunset the product in April 2024... it is not planning to invest in new news-related products.'
claims.source: TechCrunch, 'Facebook plans to shut down its news tab in the US and Australia'
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Michigan Chronicle
entities.description: Detroit weekly founded 1936 by John H. Sengstacke; a Sengstacke-chain paper now owned by Real Times Inc.; noted for early pro-labor, pro-Democratic editorial stance.

claims.claim: Founded in 1936 by John H. Sengstacke (as the Detroit Chronicle); first editor Louis E. Martin was sent to Detroit on June 6, 1936 with a $5 raise over his $15/week Chicago Defender salary, $10 cash and a one-way bus ticket; first issue circulation was 5,000.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia and Newspapers.com archive description agree on 1936 founding, Martin's June 6 arrival, and the raise/bus-ticket details.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Circulation grew from ~900 paid at Martin's arrival to 15,000 weekly by 1940 and topped 25,000 in 1945; the paper drew national attention for a "radical" pro-organized-labor and pro-Democratic stance unusual among Black papers of the era.
claims.evidence: Newspapers.com archive description gives the circulation trajectory; Wikipedia notes the pro-labor/Democratic stance.
claims.uncertainty: Medium: early circulation figures from secondary archive description.

claims.claim: James Ingram of the Michigan Chronicle was one of the negotiators in the Attica Prison uprising of September 1971.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia account.
claims.uncertainty: Low. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

claims.claim: The Chronicle is owned by Detroit-based Real Times Inc., with reported weekly circulation of 27,000 and readership of 120,000 (2015).
claims.evidence: Wikipedia infobox (2015 figures).
claims.uncertainty: Medium: 2015 figures from single secondary source.

entities.name: Moguldom Media Group
entities.description: Digital media company founded by Jamarlin Martin; built and later sold Black-culture sites Bossip, MadameNoire, and HipHopWired to Urban One.

claims.claim: Jamarlin Martin founded and led Moguldom Media Group, building Bossip, MadameNoire, HipHopWired, and The Atlanta Post (launched March 2010) into a multi-brand digital platform; he later sold three brands to Urban One (iONE Digital).
claims.evidence: Moguldom.com: Martin 'grew Moguldom Media Group into a multiple-brand digital media and entertainment platform, selling three brands to Urban One NASDAQ: UONEK'; Adweek (2010): 'Moguldom Media, the company behind Bossip.com and Hip-Hop Wired, today announced the launch of The Atlanta Post.'
claims.source: Moguldom.com, 'The Moguldom Nation Editorial Staff'; Adweek (2010)
claims.uncertainty: Founder bio (primary, self-interested) for the growth narrative; brand list corroborated by Black Enterprise acquisition reporting.

claims.claim: Moguldom's model leaned on paid discovery marketing and first-party audience analysis to scale brands quickly — an early case of a Black publisher arbitraging platform distribution.
claims.evidence: Moguldom.com: Martin 'is often cited as a subject matter expert in paid discovery marketing, which he considers an essential element to grow multimillion-dollar digital brands in the shortest time possible.'
claims.uncertainty: Self-described strategy; effectiveness not independently verified in this pass.

entities.name: Morgan DeBaun
entities.description: Co-founder and CEO of Blavity Inc.; one of the most prominent Black women founders in digital media venture funding.

claims.claim: Morgan DeBaun co-founded Blavity in 2014 at age 24 after leaving Intuit; she and co-founder Aaron Samuels made Forbes 30 Under 30 in 2016.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'Blavity was founded by CEO Morgan DeBaun... DeBaun left Intuit, where she had worked for three years'; 'In 2016, co-founders DeBaun and Samuels were named to the Forbes 30 Under 30 list.'; Bustle: 'when DeBaun was just 24 years old.'
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: DeBaun raised Blavity's $6.5M Series A (led by GV, July 2018), sits on strategy of diversified revenue (Blavity Culture Network ad sales for publishers of color; AfroTech conferences), and has said advertisers avoid adjacency to coverage of 'Black death and violence' while Facebook flagged Blavity content as too violent.
claims.evidence: Black Enterprise (2018) on the raise; TechCrunch (2020) interview: 'advertisers and marketers do not want to spend money next to Black death and violence... There was a time when our Facebook page was even blocked.'; Digiday (2022) on the Blavity Culture Network adding seven multicultural publishers.
claims.uncertainty: Founder/company statements (primary, self-interested) for strategy and revenue claims.

entities.name: Muhammad Speaks
entities.description: Nation of Islam newspaper (1961-1975) under Elijah Muhammad; at its peak the largest Black-owned weekly in US history; predecessor lineage to The Final Call.

claims.claim: The first edition of Muhammad Speaks was published in 1961 under Elijah Muhammad (growing out of Malcolm X's New York-based Mr. Muhammad Speaks); it moved from monthly to weekly on February 12, 1965 and ran until October 1975.
claims.evidence: Final Call's own history: first edition 1961, monthly at first, weekly from Feb 1965; Black Archives of Mid-America collection dates the run 1960-1975.
claims.source: new.finalcall.com (2009 history); Black Archives of Mid-America finding aid (AC58)
claims.uncertainty: Low-medium: 1960 vs 1961 first-year discrepancy between archive and NOI account.
claims.contradictory: First year 1960 (Black Archives) vs 1961 (Final Call history).

claims.claim: Circulation grew from 800,000 to 850,000 per edition and hit 950,000 one week in 1974; the NOI operated its own four-color Goss printing press in a four-story plant.
claims.evidence: Final Call's own historical account (circulation figures and press details). Figures are self-reported.
claims.uncertainty: High: circulation is NOI self-reported, not independently audited; widely repeated but unverifiable.

claims.claim: After Elijah Muhammad's death in 1975, his son W. D. Muhammad took over the Nation and the newspaper, which was renamed (Bilalian News, later The Muslim Journal).
claims.evidence: Black Archives of Mid-America collection description documents the 1975 transition and renamings.
claims.source: Black Archives of Mid-America finding aid (AC58)
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Mutual Black Network
entities.description: National Black-audience radio news network founded by the Mutual Broadcasting System in 1972; acquired by Sheridan Broadcasting, becoming the Sheridan Broadcasting Network.

claims.claim: MBN was founded by the Mutual Broadcasting System in 1972 as the first national full-service radio network aimed at African Americans, reaching 98 affiliated stations.
claims.evidence: Mutual Black Network Wikipedia: founded 1972, 'first national full-service radio network aimed at African Americans,' 98 affiliates, initially branded Mutual Reports Network.
claims.uncertainty: 'First' conflicts with the 1954 National Negro Network unless 'full-service news network' vs 'programming service' distinction is drawn.

claims.claim: Sheridan Broadcasting bought 49% of MBN in 1976 and the remaining 51% in 1979, renaming it the Sheridan Broadcasting Network.
claims.evidence: AURN Wikipedia and Mutual Black Network Wikipedia both record the 1976/1979 purchases; BET (2008) confirms the Aug 29, 1979 date.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Nat D. Williams
entities.description: Memphis high school teacher and syndicated columnist who became a WDIA disc jockey in 1948, pioneering the 'Black appeal' radio style.

claims.claim: Williams launched 'Tan Town Jubilee' (also rendered 'Jamboree') on WDIA on October 25, 1948, one of the first US radio programs designed specifically for a Black audience.
claims.evidence: WDIA Wikipedia entry dates 'Tan Town Jubilee' to October 25, 1948; Smithsonian Folklife Festival notes the 1948 start; TeachRock lesson plan dates the hiring to October 1948; Tennessee HJR0641 (1998) confirms the 1948 'first' claims by the Tennessee legislature.
claims.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WDIA; festival.si.edu; teachrock lesson PDF; capitol.tn.gov HJR0641
claims.uncertainty: Exact date of first broadcast (Oct 25, 1948) comes from secondary sources; show title is spelled 'Jubilee' and 'Jamboree' in different sources.

claims.claim: Williams was the first publicly recognized Black disc jockey in the segregated South.
claims.evidence: Tennessee HJR0641 calls him 'the first station south of the Mason-Dixon line to air a publicly recognized black disc jockey'; TeachRock describes him as 'the first publicly known Black on-air radio personality in the segregated South.' The qualifier 'publicly recognized/known' is doing work: earlier Black radio workers existed (e.g., Jack L. Cooper, Al Benson) but outside the South.
claims.uncertainty: The 'in the South' qualifier is essential; without it the claim conflicts with Cooper (1929).

claims.claim: Williams helped create 'Black appeal radio' and the jive-talking DJ patter that led toward the urban contemporary format.
claims.evidence: Nat D. Williams Wikipedia entry: 'heralded the changing radio style which helped to create Black appeal radio, which in turn led to the urban contemporary listening format.'
claims.uncertainty: Interpretive historical claim, hard to falsify but widely repeated.

entities.name: National Association of Black Owned Broadcasters
entities.description: Trade organization founded 1976 by Eugene Jackson and others to represent Black broadcast owners; now under USBC Media Network.

claims.claim: NABOB was organized in 1976 by a small group of African-American broadcasters to establish a voice in the industry; it is the first and largest trade organization for Black station owners.
claims.evidence: BMI/NABOB: 'organized in 1976 by a small group of African-American broadcasters'; NBN Wikipedia ties founding to Eugene Jackson in Atlanta.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: NABOB/BIA's 2022 Black Owned Radio Stations Ownership & Revenue Report provided the first authoritative benchmark of Black-owned radio stations and their economic standing.
claims.evidence: BusinessWire 2022: 'prior to this report the industry did not have available an authoritative record of these stations, nor their economic standing.'
claims.uncertainty: Report itself is paywalled/gated; station counts cited from it vary in secondary reporting.

entities.name: National Black Network
entities.description: Coast-to-coast Black-owned radio news network launched in New York on July 2, 1973; merged into American Urban Radio Networks in 1991.

claims.claim: NBN launched July 2, 1973 in New York City with 25 affiliates; it was the first coast-to-coast radio network fully owned by Black Americans.
claims.evidence: NBN Wikipedia: launch July 2, 1973, 25 affiliates; BlackAmericaWeb: 'first coast-to-coast radio network fully owned by Black Americans on July 2, 1973.'
claims.uncertainty: Some sources credit Robert Pauley (white ABC/Mutual executive) as the brainchild; the Black executives who carried it through were Eugene Jackson, Sydney L. Small, and Del Raycee.

claims.claim: NBN merged with its rival Sheridan Broadcasting Network in 1991 (sources say 1991; one says by 1995) to form American Urban Radio Networks.
claims.contradictory: National Black Network Wikipedia gives 'By 1995' while AURN's own article says 1991.
claims.evidence: AURN Wikipedia: formed 1991 from SBN+NBN merger; NBN Wikipedia: 'By 1995, NBN merged with... Sheridan Broadcasting Network... to form the American Urban Radio Networks.'
claims.uncertainty: 1991 vs 1995 discrepancy between Wikipedia articles on the same merger.

entities.name: National Negro Network
entities.description: Black-oriented radio programming service founded January 20, 1954 by Chicago advertiser W. Leonard Evans Jr.; collapsed within a year.

claims.claim: The National Negro Network, founded January 20, 1954 by W. Leonard Evans Jr., was the first Black-owned radio network in the country, with programming carried on up to 45 affiliates.
claims.contradictory: BET (2008) described Sheridan's 1979 purchase of MBN as 'the beginning of the first Black-owned radio network in the world,' contradicting the NNN's 1954 primacy.
claims.evidence: National Negro Network Wikipedia, citing Broadcasting trade publication: network expected 'to reach approximately 12 million of the 15 million Negroes in America.'
claims.uncertainty: Reach figure was an expectation, not measured. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

claims.claim: The network fell apart within a year due to inadequate capital and advertiser reluctance, as agencies kept 'Negro radio' campaigns at 'test' level.
claims.evidence: NNN Wikipedia: 'fell apart within a year due to inadequate capital'; Jason Chambers, Madison Avenue and the Color Line, quoting Evans on agency reluctance.
claims.uncertainty: None material. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

entities.name: National Newspaper Publishers Association (NNPA)
entities.description: Trade association of the Black Press of America; claims 200+ Black-owned community newspapers as members. Its economic survival — ad revenue, federal ad equity — is the core of Black print economics.

claims.claim: The NNPA was founded in 1940 when John H. Sengstacke of the Chicago Defender organized Black publishers to "harmoniz[e] our energies in a common purpose for the benefit of Negro journalism"; the group first called itself the National Negro Publishers Association.
claims.evidence: The quoted purpose phrase and 1940 founding by Sengstacke are consistent across multiple secondary sources; Savannah Tribune (NNPA member) states Sengstacke founded the NNPA in 1940.
claims.source: African American Registry, "The National Newspaper Publishers Association is Founded" (aaregistry.org); Savannah Tribune via NNPA coverage
claims.uncertainty: Low; multiple sources agree on year and organizer. Exact meeting date within 1940 not verified.

claims.claim: The association was renamed the National Newspaper Publishers Association in 1956.
claims.evidence: Renaming year stated in Wikipedia-derived summaries mirrored on multiple reference sites.
claims.source: Alchetron (mirroring Wikipedia), updated Apr 25, 2026; en-academic.com (2010 Wikimedia mirror)
claims.uncertainty: Low; uncontested across sources.

claims.claim: NNPA comprises 200+ Black-owned newspapers (US and Virgin Islands) with combined readership of roughly 15-20 million, and launched NNPA Media Services (print/web ad placement and press release distribution) in 2000.
claims.evidence: Member count consistently "more than 200"; readership figures vary: 15 million (Alchetron/en-academic), 19 million (Growjo), 20 million (Savannah Tribune, nnpa.org statement). NNPA Media Services 2000 launch per Alchetron.
claims.source: nnpa.org; Savannah Tribune; Alchetron; Growjo company profile
claims.uncertainty: Medium: exact readership figure varies by source and year; all are self-reported or trade estimates, not independently audited.
claims.contradictory: 15M vs 19M vs 20M readership claims across sources.

claims.claim: In June 2019, Houston Forward Times publisher Karen Carter Richards was elected NNPA national chair, succeeding Dorothy Leavell (Chicago/Gary Crusader publisher).
claims.evidence: LA Sentinel reported Richards' election at the NNPA Legacy Awards in Cincinnati, June 28, 2019; Post News Group reported her candidacy and first-vice-chair role.
claims.source: Los Angeles Sentinel, 2019-06-28; Post News Group
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: NNPA is a trade association of more than 200 African-American-owned community newspapers in the U.S.; its 2025 national convention in Savannah, Georgia marked the 198th anniversary of the Black Press (tracing to Freedom's Journal, 1827).
claims.contradictory: Wikipedia notes NNPA's site listed 160+ member papers in 2023, below the 200+ figure the association claims.
claims.evidence: NNPA's own site and The Final Call's convention coverage; C. Nast reporting.
claims.uncertainty: Membership count is self-reported and fluctuates; 2023 listings cited 'more than 160,' suggesting the 200+ figure may include inactive or associate members.

claims.claim: Black Press leaders report severe ad-revenue losses in the anti-DEI retrenchment period, with one industry publication headlining 'Black Press Loses 80% of Revenue'; Washington Informer publisher Denise Rolark Barnes said publishers were categorized as 'the DEI bucket' in ad-buying decisions.
claims.evidence: journal-isms.com reporting, July 2026; WRC-TV news segment.
claims.uncertainty: The 80% figure appears in a headline without disclosed methodology; it reflects publishers' self-reported losses, not an audited industry study.

claims.claim: NNPA faced an internal leadership crisis in late 2025: a letter circulated by Chicago Crusader publisher Dorothy Leavell alleged staff furloughs due to cash-flow problems as of December 15, 2025, no national salesperson, and a $250,000+ annual compensation package for President/CEO Benjamin Chavis.
claims.evidence: journal-isms.com reporting on Leavell's circulated letter; Chavis did not respond to comment.
claims.uncertainty: One-sided internal allegation reported by one trade publication; not independently verified and NNPA/Chavis did not respond.

claims.claim: NNPA states its printed editions remain especially important in communities with limited broadband access, positioning print as 'the lifeblood' of the communities it serves.
claims.evidence: NNPA statement in The Madison Times, 2018, opposing newsprint tariffs.
claims.uncertainty: Advocacy statement; circulation and print-revenue data to quantify the claim were not located in this research.

claims.claim: The NNPA was founded February 29-March 2, 1940, in Chicago by John H. Sengstacke and 20 publishers as the National Negro Publishers Association (renamed the National Newspaper Publishers Association in 1956), making it the oldest association of Black-owned newspapers in the country.
claims.evidence: BlackPast.org: 'On February 29-March 2, 1940, a conference of Black newspaper owners met in Chicago and organized the National Negro Publishers Association (NNPA)... founded by 20 publishers under the leadership of John H. Sengstacke... In 1956 the organization was renamed the National Newspaper Publishers Association.'
claims.uncertainty: Low; widely corroborated.

claims.claim: NNPA membership comprises more than 200 Black-owned newspapers; the association has operated for 85 years as of 2025.
claims.contradictory: A business-data aggregator lists 'over 180 member publications'; NNPA's own site says 'more than 200 Black-owned newspapers.'
claims.evidence: nnpa.org: 'As the trade organization of the nation's Black press, NNPA serves over 200 Black-owned newspapers.' Savannah Tribune: 'the trade organization of more than 200 Black-owned newspapers... celebrating 85 years.'
claims.uncertainty: Membership counts fluctuate; treat 200 as current-order-of-magnitude.

claims.claim: NNPA reporting of federal data shows systemic ad-spend inequity: Black-owned businesses received $51 million of $5+ billion in federal advertising over five years (1.02%), and $256 million of $1.2 billion to minority-owned firms across FY 2014-2023.
claims.evidence: NNPA (March 2024): 'Black-owned businesses have only received $51 million of the more than $5 billion spent in advertising by the federal government over the last five years. That accounts for 1.02% of advertising dollars spent.' NNPA (Feb 2024, citing a GAO report): of $1.2 billion to minority-owned businesses in FYs 2014-2023, '$256 million went to Black-owned businesses.'
claims.uncertainty: Figures are as reported by NNPA from federal/GAO data; they cover federal ad spend to Black-owned businesses generally, not Black media specifically.

claims.claim: In December 2025 NNPA staff were furloughed after an internal leadership crisis described in a letter from publisher Dorothy Leavell; the trade organization's operational continuity is in question.
claims.evidence: Richard Prince's Journal-isms (Dec 26, 2025): 'NNPA Furloughs Staff Amid Leavell Letter on Drummond; ... the NNPA... has furloughed staff' in the wake of a leadership dispute.
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source (an industry columnist); outcome and resolution unknown as of 2026-09.

entities.name: New Pittsburgh Courier
entities.description: Relaunched 1967 by John H. Sengstacke after the original Courier's collapse; still publishing; owned since 2003 by Detroit-based Real Times Inc.

claims.claim: Sengstacke reopened the paper in 1967 under the new name New Pittsburgh Courier - reportedly renamed to avoid the old paper's outstanding tax bills and invoices - joining his chain of Black newspapers.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: "He reorganized the paper under a new name... to avoid paying several outstanding tax bills and invoices"; reopened 1967.
claims.uncertainty: Low; tax-bill motive is Sengstacke-era reporting. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

claims.claim: In 1974 Sengstacke appointed Hazel B. Garland editor-in-chief of the New Pittsburgh Courier, making her the first African-American woman editor of a national newspaper; the paper won the John B. Russwurm Award for best national African-American newspaper in 1976.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia quotes Sengstacke's statement on the appointment and the 1976 award.
claims.uncertainty: Low. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

claims.claim: After Sengstacke's death in 1997, the four-paper chain was held in a family trust until 2003, when it was sold for nearly $12 million to Real Times, an investor group with business and family ties to Sengstacke.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia account of the trust and 2003 sale.
claims.uncertainty: Low-medium: sale price "nearly $12 million" per single Wikipedia account. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

entities.name: New York Amsterdam News
entities.description: Harlem weekly founded 1909; among the leading Black weeklies for over a century; one of about 50 Black-owned papers at its founding and still publishing.

claims.claim: Founded December 4, 1909 by James Henry Anderson in the San Juan Hill neighborhood with $10, six sheets of paper and a pencil; sold for 2 cents from his home at 132 West 65th Street; one of about 50 Black-owned newspapers in the US at the time.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia and African American Registry give Dec 4, 1909 founding, $10 capital, 2-cent price; Moguldom cites the New York Times on the six-page handwritten first edition.
claims.source: Wikipedia (New York Amsterdam News); African American Registry; Moguldom, 2022-07-18
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: In its heyday circulation exceeded 100,000; by the mid-1940s it was one of the four leading Black newspapers in the country alongside the Pittsburgh Courier, the Afro-American, and the Chicago Defender.
claims.evidence: African American Registry states both claims.
claims.uncertainty: Medium: heyday circulation figure is a secondary estimate.

claims.claim: Ownership changed hands: Anderson sold to Sadie Warren in 1926; resold ~1935-36 to physicians Dr. Clilan B. Powell and Dr. Phillip M. H. Savory; in 1971 Powell sold to an all-Black group led by Manhattan Borough President Percy E. Sutton and Clarence B. Jones.
claims.evidence: African American Registry (1926, 1935-36 sales); Moguldom (1971 sale to Sutton/Jones group after failed employee buyout).
claims.uncertainty: Low-medium; 1935 vs 1936 sale year varies.

claims.claim: Under Powell and Savory the paper became the first Black newspaper with all departments unionized; contributors included W. E. B. Du Bois, Roy Wilkins and Adam Clayton Powell Jr.; Marvel Cooke became its first female news reporter.
claims.evidence: African American Registry lists unionization first, contributors, and Cooke.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: The paper's 1916-1938 headquarters at 2293 Seventh Avenue in Harlem is a National Historic Landmark (designated 1976).
claims.evidence: National Park Service landmark nomination form (NHLS 76001247) documents 1909 founding and 1916-1938 occupancy.
claims.source: NPS NRHP nomination form; Wikipedia (New York Amsterdam News Building)
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Nielsen
entities.description: Dominant U.S. TV and audio audience-measurement company; its ratings function as ad-buying currency. Repeatedly criticized for undercounting Black (and Hispanic/young) audiences.

claims.claim: The Media Rating Council suspended Nielsen's national (and local) TV ratings accreditation in September 2021 after an audit found Nielsen undercounted viewers during the pandemic (panel maintenance failures; out-of-home software error); national accreditation was restored in April 2023 after a 19-month suspension.
claims.contradictory: Wikipedia dates the loss to 2022 rather than September 2021.
claims.evidence: NewsLab, MarTech, Advanced Television reporting on the MRC decision and restoration.
claims.uncertainty: Low; dates and causes consistently reported.

claims.claim: In January 2025 Nielsen's Big Data + Panel national TV measurement received MRC accreditation — combining its panel with set-top-box, smart TV, and streaming data from 45M+ homes; Nielsen endorsed it as currency for the 2025 upfront.
claims.evidence: AdTechRadar and VideoWeek reporting on the MRC accreditation announcement.
claims.uncertainty: Low for the accreditation; whether the hybrid method resolves minority undercounting remains an open, contested question.

claims.claim: Nielsen reports Black Americans are the heaviest media consumers in the U.S. — more than 81 hours per week across TV, radio and internet (92+ hours for those 65+); 92% of the Black population listens to traditional radio at least weekly.
claims.evidence: Nielsen's 'Seeing and believing' representation report as reported by Research Live and BusinessGhana/NBC News.
claims.uncertainty: Company-reported research figures; reported secondhand through media outlets rather than the primary Nielsen release.

claims.claim: Measurement methodology critiques are longstanding: the Council for Research Excellence flagged chronic shortages of Black, Hispanic and young diary participants; civil-rights groups challenged the Local People Meter for undercounting minorities, prompting Nielsen to appoint a task force chaired by former Congresswoman Cardiss Collins.
claims.evidence: Poynter (2013) on CRE diary research; TV Technology on the LPM task force.
claims.uncertainty: Low for the existence of the critiques and task force; magnitude of the undercount in each era was contested by Nielsen.

entities.name: Okayplayer
entities.description: Black music-and-culture digital publisher named by BET as exposed to AI-search traffic risk; founding/ownership details unverified here.

claims.claim: BET (2025) named Okayplayer among Black-owned digital outlets vulnerable to Google AI Overview traffic loss, noting such sites 'depend on every single visitor to stay alive.'
claims.evidence: BET: 'Black-owned sites like The Grio, Blavity, Okayplayer, AfroTech, and countless local newsrooms don't have that cushion.'
claims.source: BET, 'When Google AI Summarizes, Black Websites Pay the Price'
claims.uncertainty: Low for the naming; the piece is analysis, not a traffic audit.

claims.claim: Founding and ownership details for Okayplayer were not verified in this research pass.
claims.evidence: No source captured.
claims.uncertainty: HIGH: commonly associated with The Roots, but do not assert founding date or ownership without verification.

entities.name: Opportunity: A Journal of Negro Life
entities.description: Official journal of the National Urban League (1923-1949); Harlem Renaissance literary hub under Charles S. Johnson; famed for its 1924-1927 literary contests.

claims.claim: Opportunity was the official journal of the National Urban League, first published in 1923; its name came from the NUL slogan "Not alms, but opportunity"; first editor-in-chief was Charles S. Johnson.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia and Grolier Club exhibition agree on 1923, NUL organ, slogan origin, and Johnson.
claims.source: Wikipedia (Opportunity: A Journal of Negro Life); Grolier Club exhibition
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Its literary contests (1924-1927), with glamorous award dinners, launched or burnished the reputations of Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, Sterling Brown, Arna Bontemps and Countee Cullen; Countee Cullen became assistant editor in 1926.
claims.evidence: Lehigh University scalar project on the contests; Wikipedia on Cullen.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Under Johnson circulation rose to 11,000 in 1928; Johnson left for the Fisk University presidency in 1928 (succeeded by Elmer Carter), after which literary emphasis diminished and the journal focused more narrowly on sociology, economics and race.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (11,000 in 1928; Carter succession) and Lehigh (1928 shift).
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Published monthly from 1923 to 1942, then quarterly through 1949, when it ceased.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (monthly 1923-1942, quarterly through 1949); UPenn Online Books serial record (began 1923, ran until 1949).
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Oprah Winfrey
entities.description: Media figure whose Harpo joint venture created OWN.

claims.claim: Oprah Winfrey founded OWN through Harpo; she is the namesake, founder, and contracted face of the network.
claims.evidence: OWN is 'founded by television personality Oprah Winfrey' and 'named after Oprah Winfrey'; the JV is between Warner Bros. Discovery and Harpo Productions/Studios.
claims.uncertainty: Low [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

entities.name: OWN (Oprah Winfrey Network)
entities.description: Oprah Winfrey Network; lifestyle cable network launched 2011 via Discovery/Harpo JV.

claims.claim: OWN launched January 1, 2011, replacing the Discovery Health Channel, as a 50/50 joint venture between Discovery Communications and Harpo Inc., named for Oprah Winfrey.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia OWN: launched Jan 1, 2011, replacing Discovery Health; initially 50/50 JV between Warner Bros. Discovery's networks division and Harpo Productions. Discovery 8-K (Aug 2010): JV amendment set launch on or before Jan 1, 2011; Discovery raised funding commitment from $100M to $189M.
claims.source: Discovery 8-K filing (secdatabase); Wikipedia: Oprah Winfrey Network
claims.uncertainty: Low

claims.claim: Discovery increased its stake to 73% in 2017 and to 95% in December 2020, leaving Harpo a 'significant' minority stakeholder; Winfrey remains contracted with the channel.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia OWN: 'Initially a 50/50 joint venture, Discovery acquired a larger stake in the network in 2017 and again in December 2020, when Discovery increased its ownership in OWN from 73% to 95%.'
claims.uncertainty: Low [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

claims.claim: OWN debuted in ~80 million homes and was available to ~81.9M pay-TV households (70.3%) as of Feb 2015; it targets a female audience with a focus on African Americans.
claims.evidence: OWN press materials (2011): debuted Jan 1, 2011 in ~80M homes on Discovery Health's channel slot. Wikipedia: ~81.9M households Feb 2015.
claims.uncertainty: Low

entities.name: Paramount Skydance
entities.description: Merged media conglomerate (Skydance + Paramount, $8.4B deal) led by CEO David Ellison; owner of BET Media Group since the merger.

claims.claim: Skydance Media merged with Paramount in an $8.4 billion deal, with the board approving the deal in July 2024 and David Ellison becoming chairman/CEO in 2025.
claims.evidence: Black Enterprise, Hot97, Wikipedia reporting.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: PBS Black programming strands
entities.description: The public-broadcasting strand lineage for Black programming, from 1968 to today.

claims.claim: PBS's Black public-television lineage runs from Black Journal (1968) through Soul! (WNET, 1968-1973) to current national strands including 'Finding Your Roots with Henry Louis Gates, Jr.' (premiered 2012), plus strand/anthology programming such as Independent Lens, American Experience, and American Masters that regularly feature Black-centered documentaries.
claims.evidence: AAPB/Thirteen document the Black Journal era and a curated 'Black Journal and Soul!' exhibit. Finding Your Roots premiered 2012 with Gates as host — widely known but not directly re-verified in this pass.
claims.source: THIRTEEN/WNET; AAPB (general knowledge for current strands)
claims.uncertainty: Current-strand details not directly sourced in this research pass; needs strand-level verification.

entities.name: Percy Sutton
entities.description: Civil rights attorney, former Manhattan borough president, and media-ownership pioneer who founded Inner City Broadcasting Corporation.

claims.claim: Sutton founded Inner City Broadcasting Corporation in 1970 with a group of Black shareholders, starting with the purchase of WLIB (AM) in New York.
claims.contradictory: Sources variously date the WLIB purchase to 1970, 1971, or 1972.
claims.evidence: HistoryMakers finding aid (Pierre Sutton): 'cofounded the Inner City Broadcasting Corporation (ICBC) in New York City in 1970'; Adweek: 'Inner City purchased WLIB in 1970'; Journal-isms (NYT obituary reprint): 'In 1971 Mr. Sutton and others bought WLIB... making it the first black-owned station in New York City.'
claims.source: thehistorymakers.org A2013_314 finding aid; adweek.com; journal-isms.com
claims.uncertainty: Purchase year given as 1970, 1971, or 1972 across sources.

claims.claim: Under Sutton, Inner City grew to 18 stations plus cable and the Apollo Theater, making it the second-largest broadcaster targeting a Black audience after Radio One.
claims.evidence: Final Call: 'ICBC at one-time owned 18 radio stations across the nation and the famed Apollo Theater'; 'ICBC was the second-largest broadcasting company targeting a Black audience after ... Radio One.'
claims.uncertainty: 18 is the peak figure reported; exact year of peak not specified.

entities.name: Philadelphia Tribune
entities.description: Founded 1884; the oldest continuously published African-American newspaper in the United States; led by president/CEO Robert W. Bogle.

claims.claim: Founded November 27, 1884 by Christopher James Perry Sr.; it is the oldest continuously published African-American newspaper in the United States.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia infobox and text; 2024 Congressional Record tribute on its 140th anniversary; 1991 Pennsylvania Historical & Museum Commission marker inscription.
claims.source: Wikipedia (Philadelphia Tribune); Congressional Record, 2024-11-22; HMdb.org marker record
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Led by publisher/president/CEO Robert W. Bogle; the Tribune has won the NNPA's John B. Russwurm Award for "Best Newspaper" seven times since 1995.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia and African American Registry both report seven Russwurm wins since 1995.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: It publishes Tuesday-Friday and Sunday with reported circulation of 31,544 weekday / 23,698 Sunday (September 2020), and also publishes Tribune Magazine, Entertainment Now, Sojourner, The Learning Key and The Sunday Tribune.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia infobox and text (2020 figures).
claims.uncertainty: Medium: 2020 circulation figure from single secondary source; figures age quickly.

entities.name: Pittsburgh Courier
entities.description: Pittsburgh weekly that became one of the largest and most influential Black newspapers in America in the 1930s-40s (14 national editions, Double V campaign), then declined and ceased in 1966.

claims.claim: The Pittsburgh Courier was founded in Pittsburgh (published from 1907 per multiple sources; Wikipedia infobox lists incorporation May 10, 1910) by Edwin Nathaniel Harleston, Edward Penman, Hepburn Carter, Scott Wood Jr., and Harvey Tanner.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia article text says "published in Pittsburgh from 1907 until October 22, 1966" while its infobox lists founding May 10, 1910; Nieman Reports timeline lists "Pittsburgh Courier, 1907"; University of Pittsburgh documentary titled "1907-1965".
claims.source: Wikipedia (Pittsburgh Courier); Nieman Reports, "Timeline: Milestones of the Black Press in the U.S."; Pitt Chronicle, 2010-01-19
claims.uncertainty: Medium: founding year 1907 vs incorporation date 1910 differ across sources; founders' names from Wikipedia infobox only.
claims.contradictory: 1907 (article text, Nieman, Pitt) vs May 10, 1910 (Wikipedia infobox).

claims.claim: Under editor Robert Lee Vann (1910-1933, 1935-1940), the Courier became one of the leading Black newspapers in the US; Vann died in 1940.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia infobox lists Vann's editorship tenure; African American Registry states Vann died in 1940; Encyclopedia.com profile confirms 1930s national-leader status.
claims.uncertainty: Low for tenure and death year.

claims.claim: At its peak the Courier reached roughly 350,000-400,000 circulation (357,000 in 1947 per Wikipedia infobox; 400,000 peak per University of Pittsburgh; 268,447 in 1951 per Wikipedia's Pennsylvania newspaper list), printed in 14 national editions.
claims.evidence: Three different circulation figures from three sources; 14 national editions per Pitt Chronicle.
claims.source: Wikipedia; Pitt Chronicle, 2010-01-19; Wikipedia "List of African American newspapers in Pennsylvania"
claims.uncertainty: Medium-high: peak figure varies 350k-400k by source; figures are not independently audited.

claims.claim: In 1942 the Courier launched the Double V campaign - demanding victory against fascism abroad and racism at home - which became a national Black-press cause endorsed by many Black newspapers.
claims.evidence: Nieman Reports timeline: "in 1942 launched the Double V campaign - promoting the fight for democracy overseas as well as against discrimination at home."
claims.source: Nieman Reports, "Timeline: Milestones of the Black Press in the U.S."
claims.uncertainty: Low for existence and year; exact start date within 1942 not verified from this source.

claims.claim: The Courier declined in the 1950s-60s and was purchased by John H. Sengstacke (Chicago Defender publisher) - reported as 1965 by Wikipedia/Encyclopedia.com, as 1966 by the African American Registry - ceased publication October 22, 1966, and reopened in 1967 as the New Pittsburgh Courier.
claims.evidence: New Pittsburgh Courier Wikipedia: purchased 1965, reopened 1967 under new name; African American Registry: "in 1966, the Sengstacke Group bought it"; Pittsburgh Courier Wikipedia: ceased Oct 22, 1966.
claims.source: Wikipedia (New Pittsburgh Courier; Pittsburgh Courier); Encyclopedia.com; African American Registry
claims.uncertainty: Medium: acquisition year 1965 vs 1966 is disputed between sources.
claims.contradictory: Acquisition year 1965 (Wikipedia, Encyclopedia.com) vs 1966 (African American Registry).

claims.claim: The Pittsburgh Courier was founded on May 10, 1910; under publisher Robert L. Vann it became one of America's most influential Black newspapers, peaking at 350,000-450,000 circulation in the 1940s with 14 national editions.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: founded May 10, 1910; 'By the 1940s, the Courier had a circulation of 350,000, with 14 national editions.' Pittsburgh's Chronicle: 'at its peak, the Pittsburgh Courier was reaching 450,000 readers weekly.' E&P: 'under the leadership of Robert L. Vann, the Courier became one of America's most influential black newspapers.'
claims.uncertainty: Circulation figures (350k vs 450k) differ by source; both are period-peak claims.

claims.claim: The paper collapsed financially in 1965 under owner John H. Sengstacke and ceased publication on October 22, 1966; Sengstacke bought it and relaunched it as the New Pittsburgh Courier in 1967.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'The Courier experienced a financial collapse in 1965 and ceased publication on October 22, 1966. Sengstacke bought the paper and relaunched it as the New Pittsburgh Courier in 1967.'
claims.uncertainty: None material. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

claims.claim: In 2003 the Sengstacke chain (including the New Pittsburgh Courier) was sold to Real Times for approximately $12 million, consolidating remaining Black dailies/weeklies under new ownership.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (New Pittsburgh Courier): 'In 2003, Sengstacke's chain of newspapers was sold to Real Times, a new Black-owned company, for approximately $12 million.'
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source; price is approximate.

claims.claim: The paper's run is substantially preserved: ProQuest digitized the Pittsburgh Courier (1911-2010) for institutional subscribers; Newspapers.com offers the Pittsburgh Courier (1911-2015) paywalled; the P.L. Prattis papers at the University of Pittsburgh contain Courier financial reports, drafts, scrapbooks, and photographs.
claims.evidence: UW-Madison catalog: ProQuest Historical Black Newspapers coverage 'Pittsburgh Courier (1911-2010)'. Newspapers.com: 'Pittsburgh Courier 1911-2015.' Pittsburgh Chronicle: Pitt opened the Percival L. Prattis papers — 'financial reports, drafts, scrapbooks, and photographs from his time at the Courier.'
claims.uncertainty: Digitization coverage has gaps; the national vs. local edition question (see ProQuest entity) applies here too.

entities.name: Print distribution contraction
entities.description: Structural collapse of newsstand/wholesale distribution and print ad revenue that has closed or hollowed out Black weeklies and general-market papers alike, forcing Black publishers toward digital or event models.

claims.claim: Around 2,000 newspapers closed or were transformed in the 15 years before 2018, with newsprint cost spikes (2018 tariffs) hitting Black-owned weeklies especially hard given thin margins.
claims.evidence: NNPA statement in The Madison Times (2018), citing industry closure figures and opposing newsprint tariffs.
claims.uncertainty: The 2,000 figure is an industry-wide estimate repeated in an advocacy statement; Black-press-specific closure counts were not located.

claims.claim: In February 2026 two legacy Black papers closed — the Portland Skanner (founded 1965 by Bernie Foster) and a Richmond paper — citing declining revenue and digital challenges; nonprofit Onyx Impact responded with a $500,000 commitment to Black-owned media including NNPA.
claims.evidence: C. Nast reporting; journal-isms.com.
claims.uncertainty: Low for the closures as reported; Onyx Impact commitment is a first-party announcement.

entities.name: ProQuest Historical Black Newspapers
entities.description: The dominant commercial digitization vendor for historic Black newspapers; paywalled access via institutional subscription, with coverage gaps and national-vs-local edition issues.

claims.claim: ProQuest Historical Black Newspapers offers full-page images and searchable text (XML and image search) for major Black newspapers, delivered through institutional subscriptions rather than direct consumer access.
claims.evidence: Furman University library guide: 'This database covers both full-page images and searchable text (with XML and image search), covering all articles, editorials, advertisements, images, cartoons, obituaries, and more.' University of Wisconsin-Madison catalog entry marks it 'SUBSCRIPTION'.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: One library's coverage list names 12 titles: Amsterdam News (1922-1993), Baltimore Afro-American (1893-2010), Chicago Defender (1910-1975), Cleveland Call and Post (1934-1991), Los Angeles Sentinel (1934-2010), New York Age (1887-1953), Norfolk Journal and Guide (1916-2003), Philadelphia Tribune (1912-2010), Pittsburgh Courier (1911-2010), Atlanta Daily World (1931-2010), Michigan Chronicle (1939-2010), Cleveland Call and Post (1934-2010).
claims.evidence: Furman library guide coverage list with title-by-title date ranges ending in 1991-2010.
claims.uncertainty: Coverage reflects that library's licensed package; ProQuest packages vary by institution, and runs have gaps (e.g., Defender only through 1975 in this listing).

claims.evidence: Librarian Lisa Louis Cooke: 'the Chicago Defender in ProQuest is the national edition, not the Chicago city edition,' as one of several digitization surprises in her own research.
claims.uncertainty: Secondary claim from a single researcher's write-up; needs catalog verification.

entities.name: Reach Media
entities.description: Media company co-founded by Tom Joyner in 2003 to own his syndicated show; majority-owned by Urban One since 2004.

claims.claim: Joyner launched Reach Media in 2003 with David Kantor (ex-ABC Radio Networks) to own The Tom Joyner Morning Show; Radio One bought a 53% stake in November 2004 for $56.1 million cash and stock, later increasing to 80%.

claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Readex African American Newspapers, 1827-1998
entities.description: The leading commercial full-text Black-newspaper archive (350+ titles, 1827-1998); the paywalled counterpart to Chronicling America's free access.

claims.claim: Readex's African American Newspapers, 1827-1998 provides full-text, searchable digital editions of 350+ publications from 35 states, spanning 1827-1998, beginning with Freedom's Journal.
claims.evidence: LOC subscription-databases guide: 'African American Newspapers, 1827-1998: An Readex digital collection... 350+ publications from 35 states, spanning from 1827 to 1998... The collection features Black newspapers from Freedom's Journal to the Chicago Defender.'
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: Series 1 covers 280 newspapers (1827-1998) and Series 2 adds 75+ newspapers (1835-1956), sourced from the Wisconsin Historical Society, the Library of Congress, the American Antiquarian Society, and the Schomburg Center.

claims.uncertainty: None material.
