claims.evidence: The LOC guide files the collection under 'Subscription Databases' and 'Subscription Resources' tabs.
claims.uncertainty: None.

entities.name: Real Times Inc.
entities.description: Detroit-based Black-owned media holding company that bought the four-paper Sengstacke newspaper chain in 2003; current owner of the New Pittsburgh Courier, Michigan Chronicle and Atlanta Daily World.

claims.claim: In 2003 Real Times - a group of investors with business and family ties to John H. Sengstacke - bought the four-paper Sengstacke chain (New Pittsburgh Courier, Michigan Chronicle, Atlanta Daily World, Tri-State Defender) for nearly $12 million after it had been held in a family trust since Sengstacke's 1997 death.
claims.evidence: New Pittsburgh Courier Wikipedia account of the trust and 2003 sale.
claims.uncertainty: Low-medium: price "nearly $12 million" from single secondary account. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

claims.claim: Real Times Inc. is listed as owner of the New Pittsburgh Courier, Michigan Chronicle and Atlanta Daily World.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia infoboxes for all three papers list Real Times Inc. as owner.
claims.source: Wikipedia (New Pittsburgh Courier; Michigan Chronicle; Atlanta Daily World)
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Revolt
entities.description: Black-owned music and culture media company founded by Sean Combs in 2013; after his 2024 exit, employees became its largest shareholder group.

claims.evidence: Wikipedia Revolt: as part of Comcast's NBCU arrangement, Comcast solicited minority-network proposals (Apr 2011) and announced distribution for Revolt (Feb 2012); debut Oct 21, 2013. Maxine Waters-led congressional pressure documented.
claims.uncertainty: Low [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

claims.uncertainty: Low

claims.source: AfroTech; Black Enterprise, 'Diddy May Be Down Bad, But He Did Secure His Bag'
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Richelieu Dennis
entities.description: Founder of Shea Moisture/Sundial Brands; acquirer of Essence and co-founder of Group Black; central figure in Black media ownership consolidation.

claims.claim: Richelieu Dennis founded Sundial Brands (Shea Moisture), sold it to Unilever in 2017 for a reported $1.6B, then founded Essence Ventures (2017) and co-founded Group Black (June 2021).
claims.evidence: Journal-isms (2018) on Essence Ventures' 2017 creation and the Unilever sale; Adweek: Dennis 'sold his personal care company, Sundial Brands, to Unilever in 2017 for $1.6 billion'; AfroTech: Group Black 'co-founded in June 2021 by Richelieu Dennis, Bonin Bough, and Travis Montaque.'
claims.uncertainty: The $1.6B Unilever figure was widely reported though official terms were undisclosed.

claims.contradictory: Group Black claims Dennis agreed in January 2024 to convert the disputed debt to equity — the obligation is contested.
claims.evidence: Adweek (2025): Dennis 'left the collective shortly after' summer 2024; AfroTech (2025) on the May 2025 lawsuit and June countersuit.
claims.uncertainty: Litigation allegations are disputed and unresolved as of reporting.

entities.name: Robert L. Johnson
entities.description: Former cable-industry lobbyist who founded BET in 1980 with co-founder Sheila Johnson.

claims.claim: Robert L. Johnson, a former lobbyist for the cable industry from Freeport, Illinois, founded BET; he secured a $15,000 loan and a $500,000 investment from media executive John Malone to start it.
claims.evidence: After stepping down as a lobbyist for the cable industry, Robert L. Johnson acquired a $15,000 loan and $500,000 investment from John Malone to start the network; he is named as founder (with Sheila Johnson as co-founder in the infobox).
claims.uncertainty: Low

claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'In 2005, Johnson retired from the network, turning over his titles of president and chief executive officer to former BET vice president Debra L. Lee.' Black Enterprise says 2006.
claims.uncertainty: Retirement year reported as 2005 or 2006.

claims.evidence: Black Enterprise: 'The sale of the network made the Johnsons America's first Black billionaires.'
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source; claim widely repeated but not independently documented here.

entities.name: Roland Martin
entities.description: Veteran journalist and founder of the Black Star Network, a free donor- and ad-supported Black-owned streaming network.

claims.claim: Roland Martin, a veteran broadcaster, launched the daily digital show #RolandMartinUnfiltered (~2018) and, on its third anniversary, launched the free Black-owned OTT Black Star Network on September 2, 2021.
claims.evidence: Final Call/NNPA (2021): Martin 'announced his new network on the third anniversary of #RolandMartinUnfiltered'; Spectacular Mag: 'Black Star Network was launched by veteran journalist Roland Martin on September 2, 2021.'

claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Say Brother / Basic Black
entities.description: Longest-running Black public-affairs TV program (Boston, 1968-present).

claims.evidence: AAPB special collection (WGBH): Say Brother (1968-1997) premiered three months after King's assassination; became Basic Black in 1998, title felt more inclusive of women. Wikipedia Basic Black: created 1968; reflects concerns and culture of African Americans.
claims.source: American Archive of Public Broadcasting (WGBH special collection); Wikipedia: Basic Black
claims.uncertainty: Low

claims.uncertainty: Low

entities.name: Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture
entities.description: The New York Public Library's research library devoted to the global Black experience; the single largest public repository of Black print media history in the United States.

claims.claim: The Schomburg Center holds more than 400 Black newspapers and over 1,000 periodicals from around the world, plus the Ernest D. Kaiser Index of Black Resources with roughly 179,000 citations to articles in Black magazines and newspapers, some long defunct.
claims.evidence: Profile of the Center's General Research and Reference Collections: 'more than 125,000 volumes and 85,000 microforms... The collection offers readers more than 400 Black newspapers and over 1,000 periodicals from around the world... the Ernest D. Kaiser Index to Black Resources, a file of over 179,000 citations to articles in thousands of issues of Black magazines and newspapers, some of which ceased publication decades ago.'
claims.pub_date: unknown (page archived; figures may be dated)
claims.source: tbmv3.theblackmarket.com profile of the Schomburg Center
claims.uncertainty: Source page is stale (last updated many years ago); counts likely understate current holdings. Figures need confirmation against NYPL's current catalog.

claims.claim: The Center's collections won international acclaim in 1926 when Arturo Alfonso Schomburg's personal collection was added to the NYPL 135th Street Branch's Division of Negro Literature, History and Prints; the division was renamed for Schomburg in 1940 and designated a research library in 1972.
claims.evidence: Zinn Education Project description drawn from the Schomburg Center website: collections 'first won international acclaim in 1926 when the personal collection of the distinguished Black scholar and bibliophile Arturo Alfonso Schomburg was added... The division was renamed in his honor in 1940, and in 1972 it was designated as one of the Research Libraries of the New York Public Library.'
claims.uncertainty: Low; consistent with NYPL's own institutional history.

claims.claim: KNOWN LOSS: Two or three scrapbooks on Marcus Garvey went missing around 1960 from the Schomburg Center's scrapbook collection (296 volumes assembled by staff between the 1920s and 1960s from clippings of Black newspapers including the Afro-American, Chicago Defender, Pittsburgh Courier, and Negro World).
claims.evidence: NYPL Archives & Manuscripts finding aid for the Schomburg Center scrapbooks: 'Two or three scrapbooks on Marcus Garvey went missing around 1960.' The scrapbooks contain clippings from African American newspapers such as the Afro-American (Baltimore), Chicago Defender, Pittsburgh Courier, and Negro World.
claims.source: archives.nypl.org finding aid, Schomburg Center Manuscripts, Archives and Rare Books Division
claims.uncertainty: Exact number (two vs. three) and circumstances of loss are not recorded in the finding aid.

claims.claim: Many Schomburg holdings are digitized and available online; in-person archival access is through NYPL's research-library procedures.
claims.evidence: Zinn Education Project: 'Many of the items in the Schomburg Center's collections have been digitized and are available online' with a link to the digital collection.
claims.uncertainty: General statement; specific digitization scope for media holdings not quantified here.

entities.description: Pittsburgh-based Black-owned broadcast company founded 1972 by Ronald and Judith Davenport; acquired MBN and became co-owner of AURN before losing its stake in 2016.

claims.uncertainty: Acquisition reported only in bio/secondary sources; terms and exact date unverified.

entities.name: Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture
entities.description: The Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture; joint owner and physical home of the Johnson Publishing Company Archive.

entities.name: Soul Train media library
entities.description: The Soul Train television library (1,100+ episodes): preserved through corporate acquisition by BET, not through a public archive — the commercial-consolidation survival/preservation model.

claims.claim: The Soul Train media library comprises more than 1,100 television episodes and 40 specials (1970s-2000s), described by BET as 'one of the largest libraries of African American music-oriented content in the world.'

claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.uncertainty: Characterization is analysis of the stated deal rationale; researcher access conditions are unconfirmed.

entities.name: St. Louis American
entities.description: St. Louis weekly founded 1928; the city's only continuously published Black newspaper; converted to a free weekly under Donald Suggs (owner since 1981/84) and claims to be Missouri's largest weekly.

claims.claim: First issue appeared March 17, 1928, founded by Judge Nathan B. Young Jr. and Black businessmen including Homer G. Phillips as an eight-page paid tabloid with circulation just over 2,000.
claims.evidence: Publisher Donald Suggs' 95th-anniversary account (Word In Black) and Decoding STL (Missouri Historical Society-sourced) agree on founders, date, format and circulation.
claims.uncertainty: Low-medium.

claims.source: Wikipedia (The St. Louis American); Word In Black, 2023-03
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: The paper reports 70,000+ copies distributed free at 845+ locations each Thursday and claims status (since 2012) as the single largest weekly newspaper in Missouri.
claims.evidence: Company profile via RocketReach (70,000 copies, 845 locations, 2012 largest-weekly claim); Wikipedia notes the claim as citation-needed.
claims.uncertainty: High: largest-weekly claim is self-reported and flagged citation-needed on Wikipedia.

entities.name: Teenie Harris Archive (Carnegie Museum of Art)
entities.description: The photographic archive of Pittsburgh Courier photographer Charles 'Teenie' Harris, held by the Carnegie Museum of Art: the visual record of a Black newspaper's 40-year run.

claims.claim: Charles 'Teenie' Harris was a staff and freelance photographer for the Pittsburgh Courier for roughly four decades, building a photo-historical record of Black life in Pittsburgh.
claims.evidence: Historic Pittsburgh: 'As a staff and freelance photographer for the Pittsburgh Courier for over four decades, Charles “Teenie” Harris amassed a photo-historical record of the African American community in Pittsburgh, nearly unrivaled by any other.'
claims.uncertainty: Low; widely corroborated.

claims.claim: The Teenie Harris Archive is held by the Carnegie Museum of Art and accessible through the Historic Pittsburgh digital portal.
claims.evidence: Historic Pittsburgh's dedicated collection page 'Teenie Harris Archive: Carnegie Museum of Art Collection.'
claims.uncertainty: None material.

entities.name: Telecommunications Act of 1996
entities.description: The 1996 federal deregulatory law: the structural shock that consolidated Black radio/TV ownership and defined the modern survival landscape.

claims.claim: Since the 1996 Telecommunications Act, the number of radio station owners has decreased by at least 1,100 (a ~30% decline), as ownership caps were relaxed.
claims.evidence: Congressional Record (House, vol. 149): 'the number of radio station owners has decreased by at least 1,100, representing a 30 percent decline.'
claims.uncertainty: Figure reflects early-2000s data.

claims.claim: Minority broadcasters fell from 173 (1991) to 169 (1997) to 149 (2001), per Kofi Ofori's 'Radio Local Market Consolidation and Minority Ownership' report cited by Black Enterprise.
claims.evidence: Black Enterprise 'Battle for the Airwaves' (2003) citing Ofori: 'in 1991 there were 173 minority-owned broadcasters. By 1997, however, that number dropped to 169, and by 2001 was down to 149.'
claims.uncertainty: Secondary citation of a report not directly reviewed; 'minority-owned broadcasters' is a broader category than Black-owned.

claims.claim: By 2020, Blacks owned fewer than 180 of more than 11,000 commercial radio stations (about 1.6%), per NABOB's 2020 statement.

claims.claim: Clear Channel went from ~86 stations in 1996 to ~1,200 after the Act, with about 76 targeting Black/urban audiences — illustrating how consolidation separated Black FORMAT control from Black OWNERSHIP.

claims.uncertainty: 2003-era figures; iHeartMedia's current portfolio differs.

claims.claim: The Telecommunications Act of 1996 abolished broadcast ownership caps, triggering consolidation: Clear Channel grew from 86 stations to roughly 1,200; minority-owned broadcast facilities declined about 40% and African American ownership fell about 70% after the 1995 Minority Tax Certificate repeal and the 1996 Act.
claims.evidence: Black Enterprise: 'The act abolished broadcast ownership limits, and Clear Channel... expanded from 86 stations to 1,200 stations.' FCC-commissioner testimony cited in Black Enterprise: 'Minority-owned broadcast facilities decreased by 40%. African American ownership decreased by 70%.'
claims.uncertainty: The 40%/70% figures come from FCC-hearing panelists; causal attribution to the Act is the standard account but the precise figures rest on those testimonies.

claims.claim: Kofi Ofori's FCC-cited research found 173 minority-owned broadcasters in 1991, 169 in 1997, and 149 in 2001 — documenting the decline curve around the Act's passage.
claims.evidence: Black Enterprise: Ofori 'found 173 minority-owned broadcasters in 1991, 169 in 1997, and 149 in 2001.'
claims.uncertainty: None material on the counts; they are the cited study's figures.

claims.claim: ANALYSIS: The Act's deregulatory wave destroyed most small Black station owners and left scale-and-diversification (Urban One, BET) as the dominant survival path — the central consolidation dynamic of Black broadcast history.
claims.evidence: Synthesis of the ownership-decline data with Urban One's cross-platform growth (54 stations, syndication, cable, digital) and BET's cable-network sale model.
claims.uncertainty: Analytical framing; the ownership data support the direction, not every causal link.

claims.evidence: Talkers: 'iOne Digital's dynamic portfolio of media brands... connecting with over 24 million unique monthly visitors... The iONE portfolio is comprised of Cassius, HelloBeautiful, MadameNoire, Bossip, NewsOne, GlobalGrind, HipHopWired, BlackAmericaWeb and Elev8; plus... BlackPlanet... the all-new Urban One Podcast Network.'
claims.uncertainty: Portfolio list verified; 24M figure is a company claim.

entities.name: UWG (UniWorld Group)
entities.description: New York-based multicultural ad agency founded 1969 by Byron Lewis; one of the oldest African-American-owned agencies, now minority-owned and woman-led with WPP as a 49% strategic partner.

claims.claim: UniWorld was founded in 1969 by Byron Lewis; in 2000 Lewis sold a 49% stake to WPP as a strategic alliance, and upon retiring in 2012 sold his remaining stake to Monique Nelson and her family; the firm rebranded as UWG in 2014.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia entries for Byron Lewis and UWG Inc.; Black Enterprise histories; WPP announcement.
claims.uncertainty: Low; timeline consistent across multiple sources.

claims.claim: UWG remains operating as a minority-owned, woman-led strategic partner of the WPP network, led by CEO Monique L. Nelson.
claims.evidence: WPP's current company page for UniWorld Group; Wikipedia ownership listing (Lori-Laine Holdings 51%, WPP 49%).
claims.uncertainty: Low; confirmed by WPP's own site.

entities.name: Viacom acquisition of BET
entities.description: The 2000-2001 acquisition that ended Black ownership of BET.

claims.claim: Viacom agreed in 2000 to buy BET Holdings Inc. from Robert Johnson for $2.3 billion in stock, assuming $570 million in debt; the deal closed in 2001 with BET networks joining MTV Networks.
claims.contradictory: Some outlets report the price as $2.7 billion (NY Post via clutchpoints.com: 'acquired BET from founder Bob Jonson for $2.7 billion in 2000') or $3 billion (liquisearch.com: 'bought by media conglomerate Viacom for $3 billion'). The $2.3B figure plus $570M debt assumption = ~$2.87B enterprise value, which may explain the $2.7B figure.
claims.evidence: USA Today abstract (2000): 'Viacom has agreed to buy BET Holdings Inc from founder Robert Johnson for $2.3 billion in stock and the assumption of $570 million in debt.' BET Media Group Wikipedia: 'In 2000, Viacom announced plans to purchase BET Holdings Inc. for more than $2.3 billion... The deal closed in 2001.'
claims.source: USA Today via readabstracts.com (2000); Wikipedia: BET Media Group; THR via radiox cms
claims.uncertainty: Enterprise vs equity value confusion; widely repeated figures range $2.3B-$3B. Red-team flag: inflated deal figures repeated without sources.

claims.claim: Johnson remained as CEO of BET Holdings and Debra Lee as COO for five years after the acquisition under the deal terms.
claims.evidence: USA Today abstract: 'As part of the deal, Johnson will remain as CEO of BET Holdings while Debra Lee will continue to be COO for five years after the acquisition.'
claims.uncertainty: Low

entities.name: Viacom-DirecTV blackout (2012)
entities.description: The 2012 Viacom-DirecTV carriage blackout that took BET off air for ~20M homes.

claims.claim: In July 2012 Viacom pulled 26 of its channels — including BET, MTV, Comedy Central, Nickelodeon — from DirecTV's ~20M subscribers at midnight July 10 in a carriage-fee fight; channels were restored July 20 after a new long-term deal with undisclosed terms.
claims.evidence: VentureBeat (July 2012): 26 Viacom channels went dark on DirecTV as of midnight; dispute over carriage price. Engadget/BroadwayWorld (July 20, 2012): DirecTV and Viacom reached a new long-term agreement restoring 17+ channels including BET; terms not disclosed; deal added DirecTV Everywhere digital rights.
claims.uncertainty: Low — note: Viacom, not BET itself, was the negotiating party (ownership vs carriage).

claims.claim: The blackout (9-10 days) was the largest US programming blackout to that date and a turning point: analysts noted the distributor (DirecTV) won the PR war, changing leverage dynamics for programmers.
claims.evidence: mobilenapps: 'the size, length and scope of this programming blackout was unprecedented to date in the U.S. pay-TV industry'; Bernstein analyst Todd Juenger: 'the first time in memory, it was the distributor that won the public relations war.'
claims.uncertainty: Analyst interpretation, not fact.

entities.name: Video Advertising Bureau (VAB)
entities.description: Trade advocacy group representing TV networks (sellers). Published research asserting Nielsen massively undercounted Black and Hispanic impressions during 2021-2022 — advocacy statistics that should be treated as reported, not independently verified.

claims.claim: VAB asserted that Nielsen's errors left 30 billion ad impressions uncounted, including 7 billion Black ad impressions and 5.5 billion Hispanic ad impressions, representing $350M in ads marketers could not buy — an advocacy study based on 8 of 16 months of Nielsen data.
claims.contradictory: Nielsen disputed the VAB's methodology and maintained its data was directionally sound.
claims.evidence: HispanicAd.com summary of the VAB study; TheWrap coverage of VAB's suspension case.
claims.uncertainty: High; VAB is a seller-side advocacy group that was litigating against Nielsen; the figures extrapolate from partial data and were not independently audited.

claims.claim: VAB argued Nielsen's numbers 'significantly' undercounted Blacks, Hispanics and younger adults, especially during the pandemic, and petitioned the MRC to suspend Nielsen's accreditation.
claims.evidence: TheWrap reporting on VAB's 10-page case to the MRC.
claims.uncertainty: The petition and its demographic framing are verified; the quantitative claims remain VAB's advocacy position.

entities.name: W. Paul Coates
entities.description: Founder of Black Classic Press (1978); former Baltimore Black Panther chapter leader; prison-literacy organizer; 2024 National Book Foundation Literarian Award recipient.

claims.claim: Coates founded Black Classic Press in Baltimore in 1978; he is the father of author Ta-Nehisi Coates.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia; Publishers Weekly.
claims.source: Wikipedia (Black Classic Press; Paul Coates); Publishers Weekly, 2024
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Before publishing, he led Baltimore's Black Panther Party chapter and in 1972 founded the George Jackson Prison Movement to bring Afrocentric literature to Maryland jails and prisons.
claims.evidence: Publishers Weekly (2024 Literarian coverage); Wikipedia (Paul Coates).
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: The National Book Foundation named him the 2024 Literarian Award recipient for Outstanding Service to the American Literary Community (award presented Nov 20, 2024 by his son).
claims.evidence: Publishers Weekly announcement.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Washington Informer
entities.description: Washington, D.C. weekly founded 1964 by Calvin W. Rolark; female-owned (publisher Denise Rolark Barnes); mission-driven "positive news" Black press institution.

claims.claim: Founded October 16, 1964 by Dr. Calvin W. Rolark with $500 provided by his wife, activist-lawyer Wilhelmina Jackson Rolark; the first issue (1,000 copies) was printed in LaPlata, Maryland, and Rolark hand-distributed copies to barbershops, beauty salons, churches, Safeway stores and $10 subscribers.
claims.evidence: NNPA's 60th-anniversary account by publisher Denise Rolark Barnes and DC Preservation historic-sites entry agree on the $500, Oct 16, 1964 founding and hand-distribution details.
claims.source: nnpa.org (60th anniversary editorial); DC Preservation historic sites; Wikipedia
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: The paper is female-owned; publisher is Denise Rolark Barnes, the founder's daughter (stepdaughter of Wilhelmina Rolark), who took over the family business.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia infobox lists Barnes as publisher; National Press Club program bio confirms.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Circulation is reported around 50,000 weekly across DC, Prince George's and Montgomery counties and Northern Virginia; the paper claims 40,000 weekly print readers plus digital/newsletter/social reach. An ad-rate source lists paid circulation at 17,500.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia infobox: 50,000; National Press Club (2020): 40,000 weekly readers; MACPA ad listing: 17,500 circulation - figures conflict.
claims.source: Wikipedia; National Press Club, 2020; MACPA listing
claims.uncertainty: High: figures conflict across sources (50k vs 40k readers vs 17.5k circulation).
claims.contradictory: 50,000 (Wikipedia) vs 40,000 readers (own 2020 claim) vs 17,500 (MACPA ad listing).

claims.claim: The Informer's stated mission is to "educate, inspire and inform - and to publish positive news about African Americans."
claims.evidence: National Press Club program quoting the paper's mission; company self-description.
claims.source: National Press Club, 2020; civilsocialmedia company profile
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Watering Hole Media
entities.description: Media company founded by Democratic strategist and CNN commentator Ashley Allison; acquired The Root in October 2025.

claims.claim: Ashley Allison, through Watering Hole Media, acquired The Root on October 2, 2025, with plans for video content, expert partnerships, and in-person events.
claims.evidence: Black Enterprise (Oct 2, 2025): Allison 'purchased The Root and plans to shift the platform toward more immersive and video-based experiences.'
claims.source: Black Enterprise, "'The Root' Has Made Its Way Back To Black Ownership"
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Allison launched Watering Hole Media in 2024 to amplify diverse voices at the intersection of politics and culture; she is a former Obama staffer, Biden-Harris 2020 advisor, and CNN commentator.
claims.evidence: EURweb (2025): 'In 2024, she launched Watering Hole Media to amplify diverse voices at the intersection of politics and culture. Acquiring The Root is her first major move.'
claims.source: EURweb, 'The Root Returns to Black Ownership in Major Media Move'
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source for the 2024 founding date of Watering Hole Media.

entities.name: WBLS New York
entities.description: New York urban adult contemporary station, formerly the Black-owned Inner City flagship; now owned by MediaCo (not Black-owned).

claims.claim: WBLS (107.5 FM) hit New York airwaves in 1971 as the only Black-owned FM station in the city's history, quickly becoming the city's leading station.
claims.contradictory: Inner City Wikipedia gives 1974 for the WBLS acquisition.
claims.evidence: Final Call: 'WBLS hit the NYC airways in 1971 as the only Black owned FM station in city history.'
claims.uncertainty: Inner City Wikipedia dates the WLIB-FM purchase (renamed WBLS) to 1974 via a right of first refusal exercised after the 1972 WLIB purchase; the 1971 vs 1974 discrepancy is unresolved.

claims.claim: WBLS is currently owned by MediaCo Holding (with sister station WQHT), after passing from Inner City to YMF Media (Burkle/Johnson) in 2012.
claims.evidence: WBLS Wikipedia: 'currently owned and operated by MediaCo Holding, along with sister station WQHT'; 'previously owned by YMF Media LLC, owned jointly by investor Ronald Burkle and Magic Johnson, which had assumed control ... on October 19, 2012.'
claims.uncertainty: None on ownership chain. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

claims.claim: WBLS carries HD subchannels (HD2 'Luna 107.5' Latin pop, HD3 'One Love Radio' Caribbean), showing how HD Radio subchannels have become outlets for Black-diaspora formats on non-Black-owned signals.
claims.evidence: WBLS Wikipedia: Subchannels HD2: 'Luna 107.5 HD2' (Latin pop), HD3: 'One Love Radio' (Caribbean music).
claims.uncertainty: HD programming changes frequently; current lineup may differ.

entities.name: WDIA Memphis
entities.description: Memphis AM station that became the first radio station with an all-Black programming format; now owned by iHeartMedia (Black-formatted, not Black-owned).

claims.claim: WDIA signed on June 7, 1947 as a white-owned station airing country, light pop, and block programming; after hiring Nat D. Williams in October 1948 it shifted to Black-appeal programming and by fall 1949 was effectively all-Black programming.
claims.evidence: WDIA Wikipedia: signed on June 7, 1947, owners John Pepper and Bert Ferguson (both white), country/western and light pop format; Williams hired for Tan Town Jubilee Oct 25, 1948; MadameNoire reports that by fall 1949 the station's programming and public face was 100% Black. Note: the station itself was never Black-owned.
claims.uncertainty: The 'fall 1949 100% Black' phrasing comes from a single entertainment-site article; precise phase-in dates for the full format switch are not in primary records reviewed.

claims.claim: WDIA is commonly described as the first radio station in the country with a format designed exclusively for a Black audience; this is the standard 'first all-Black-format station' claim.
claims.evidence: Tennessee HJR0641 (1998): 'the first radio station in the country with a format designed exclusively for a black audience'; Smithsonian: 'In 1948, WDIA in Memphis became the first radio station to start moving to an all-Black programming format.'
claims.uncertainty: Competing 'firsts' exist depending on definition (format vs ownership). The Smithsonian hedge 'start moving to' reflects the gradual switch.

claims.claim: In June 1954 WDIA was licensed to increase power to 50,000 watts and moved to 1070 kHz; its signal was said to reach about 10% of the African-American population of the United States.
claims.evidence: WDIA Wikipedia: 50,000-watt license and move to 1070 kHz in June 1954; 'WDIA reached 10% of the African-American population in the United States'; TeachRock lesson repeats the 10% estimate.
claims.uncertainty: The 10% figure is a widely repeated estimate with no documented primary methodology; treat as industry lore, not a measurement.

claims.claim: WDIA is now owned by iHeartMedia, making it a Black-formatted but not Black-owned station.
claims.evidence: WDIA Wikipedia infobox/lead: 'Owned by iHeartMedia.'
claims.uncertainty: Ownership current as of last crawl; could change. [Red-team regrade 2026-09-28: sole substantive source is Wikipedia (tertiary). Needs primary or reputable secondary sourcing before it can be marked Verified.]

entities.name: WERD Atlanta
entities.description: Atlanta station bought by Jesse Blayton in 1949; the first radio station both owned and programmed by African Americans. Now defunct as WERD; frequency went dark in 2024.

claims.claim: WERD is the accepted 'first Black-owned radio station' of America, with the 1948/1949 transition from white ownership to Blayton's Black ownership being the key fact.
claims.evidence: Multiple sources (WAEC Wikipedia, AJC, Smithsonian, Halper) distinguish WDIA (first Black FORMAT, white-owned) from WERD (first Black OWNED).
claims.uncertainty: Some sources give the station's establishment as 1948 with the purchase in 1949; the 'first' claim is consensus but rests on the distinction format-vs-ownership.

claims.claim: The call sign changed to WXAP on January 3, 1972; the 860 AM signal went dark in 2024.
claims.evidence: WAEC Wikipedia; AJC (2024) reporting the signal going silent after 76 years.
claims.uncertainty: None.

entities.name: Word In Black
entities.description: The national Black-news collaboration of 10 legacy papers (2021), now a public benefit corporation (2024): the cooperative/network survival model for legacy Black print.

claims.claim: Word In Black launched June 7, 2021 (soft-launched May 2021) as a collaboration of ten Black newspapers publishing on a shared national site and newsletter, plus original content.
claims.evidence: E&P (2024): 'Founded on June 7, 2021... 10 of the nation's most prestigious Black legacy newspaper publishers joined together to launch a collaborative online news presence'; Black Enterprise (Sept 17, 2021) on the ten-paper collaboration.
claims.source: Editor & Publisher, 'Word in Black's journey from a pilot project to a public benefit corporation'; Black Enterprise (2021)
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: The collaboration is part of the Fund for Black Journalism, founded by the Local Media Association and the ten papers; seed backing included a Walton Family Foundation grant (COVID/education coverage) and a $300,000 Google News Initiative Innovation Challenge grant (Dec 2020); later funders include the Facebook Journalism Project, Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, Google News Initiative, and Local Media Consortium.
claims.evidence: E&P: 'part of the Fund for Black Journalism, founded last year by the Local Media Association (LMA) and the same 10 newspapers'; 'LMA originally received funding from the Walton Family Foundation'; localmedia.org (Dec 16, 2020): 'freshly funded with $300,000 from the Google News Initiative.'
claims.source: Editor & Publisher; localmedia.org, 'Word In Black receives $300,000 in funding from Google News Initiative Innovation Challenge'
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Word In Black was incubated inside the Local Media Foundation (a 501(c)(3)); on January 1, 2024 its assets were sold to a newly formed public benefit corporation, with the foundation remaining a shareholder.
claims.evidence: E&P (2024): 'Word in Black was initially incubated inside the Local Media Foundation (LMF)... As of January 1, 2024... the foundation has sold the assets to Word in Black's newly formed public benefit company.'
claims.source: Editor & Publisher, 'Word in Black's journey from a pilot project to a public benefit corporation'
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: The ten founding papers are: AFRO News, The Atlanta Voice, Dallas Weekly, Houston Defender, Michigan Chronicle, New York Amsterdam News, The Sacramento Observer, The Seattle Medium, The St. Louis American, and The Washington Informer.
claims.evidence: E&P (2024) lists all ten founding newspapers.
claims.source: Editor & Publisher, 'Word in Black's journey from a pilot project to a public benefit corporation'
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Word In Black was founded on June 7, 2021, by 10 legacy Black newspapers (including the Baltimore AFRO, Houston Defender, Michigan Chronicle, New Pittsburgh Courier, and St. Louis American), incubated by the Local Media Foundation.
claims.evidence: Editor & Publisher: 'On June 7, 2021, ten of the nation's most historic Black newspapers... came together to launch Word In Black... incubated within the Local Media Foundation.' The founding papers are listed by wordinblack.com: Baltimore AFRO, The Atlanta Voice, Dallas Weekly, Houston Defender, Michigan Chronicle, New Pittsburgh Courier, New York Amsterdam News, Oklahoma Eagle, Sacramento Observer, St. Louis American.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: On January 1, 2024, Word In Black converted to a public benefit corporation — the first national Black news collaboration to adopt that structure.
claims.evidence: Editor & Publisher: 'On January 1, 2024, Word In Black officially became a public benefit corporation... For the first time, the collaborative had its own independent legal structure.'
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: The collaboration was seeded by foundation and platform funding: $300,000 from the Google News Initiative, plus the Walton Family Foundation, Facebook Journalism Project, and Chan Zuckerberg Initiative.
claims.evidence: Local Media Association (2020): Word In Black received '$300,000 from the Google News Initiative... also supported by the Walton Family Foundation, Facebook Journalism Project, and Chan Zuckerberg Initiative.'
claims.uncertainty: None material; institutional announcement.

entities.name: WPP
entities.description: London-based global advertising holding company; 49% owner of UniWorld Group since 2000 — illustrating how the legacy Black agencies survived by partnering with (and partially ceding ownership to) mainstream conglomerates.

claims.claim: WPP acquired a 49% interest in UniWorld Group in June 2000 under a strategic alliance, with UniWorld continuing to operate as a separate, autonomous business.
claims.evidence: WPP's own announcement; Black Enterprise coverage.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: WURD Radio Philadelphia
entities.description: Pennsylvania's only African-American-owned talk radio station (900 AM / 96.1 FM), bought by physician Walter Lomax Jr. and run by CEO Sara Lomax-Reese.

claims.claim: WURD is Pennsylvania's only African-American-owned talk radio station, one of the few Black-owned-and-operated talk stations in the country.
claims.evidence: ONA speaker bio: 'Pennsylvania's only African-American owned talk radio station'; podcast: 'one of the only Black-owned and Black-operated talk radio stations in the country.'
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Physician Walter P. Lomax Jr. bought WURD (900 AM) in 2001/2003; his daughter Sara Lomax-Reese became president/CEO, expanded it to 96.1 FM in 2017, and co-founded URL Media.
claims.contradictory: OnWURD podcast says 2001; Wikipedia says 2003.
claims.evidence: OnWURD podcast: 'Her father, Walter P. Lomax, Jr, M.D., bought the station in 2001'; Sara Lomax-Reese Wikipedia: 'Lomax purchased WURD 900 AM in 2003'; ONA: FM expansion 2017; URL Media co-founded with S. Mitra Kalita.
claims.uncertainty: Purchase year given as 2001 and 2003 in different sources.
